#2002. Time for Koppen’s ‘plan B’ over January striker signing

News rippled out across the ‘web from sources last week that West Ham United’s transfer plans for January involved Nils Koppen revisiting his old club Rangers in an attempt to steal their striker Ryan Naderi out from under their noses. The 6’5 Czech powerhouse was involved in international duty last week as Spain ran out 2 – 0 victors over his national side.

However there’s a development today that would suggest Koppen needs a plan B: The striker’s own thoughts on leaving Scotland are revealed in Thehardtackle.com’s article this afternoon:

The 23-year-old has become an important part of Derek McInnes’ plans this season, producing nine goals and six assists in 17 appearances. His form has inevitably attracted attention, with West Ham among the clubs considering him as they look to strengthen their attack.

However, Naderi is understood to be happy at Ibrox and does not see a move to the London Stadium as an attractive proposition while West Ham remain in the second tier.”

Without their Premier League status to attract new recruits  and current languishing in ninth place  in the Championship, you’d sense West Ham have a very difficult transfer window ahead if they cannot climb back up towards the automatic promotion slots ahead of the window opening in January.

Koppen will not only need a plan B but quite possibly a C, D,E F and G.

I’ve been looking into how many England caps have been picked up by Newcastle United and Sunderland players.

So this is England Caps picked up by the players of Newcastle United and Sunderland whilst the individuals were at these clubs. Not England Caps picked up before or after their times playing on Tyneside and Wearside.

Last night England delivered a superb 3-2 away victory against Spain.

The World Cup winners very lucky that they only lost by one, England roaring into a 3-0 lead and then a trio of individual errors threatening to undermine a brilliant team performance.

In that match Lewis Hall started and was his usual brilliant self, picking up his 9th cap.

Dan Burn coming off the bench late on to win his 12th cap and help see England over the line.

Those two international appearances for the United pair in Madrid now make it 347 England Caps picked up by 44 different Newcastle United players (whilst they were also playing for NUFC).

Having a look at the Sunderland players and their stats, in the entire SAFC history only 101 England Caps have been won by 29 Mackem players..

Eight different Newcastle United players played for England during the four and a half years Eddie Howe was in charge at NUFC, with seven of them signed by him. Under Eddie Howe there was almost 70 England caps won by Newcastle United players whilst also playing for NUFC. Now Lewis Hall and Dan Burn picking up what will hopefully the the first of many under Matthias Jaissle.

Jermain Defoe picked up two England Caps nine years ago and he is the only Sunderland player to appear for England since 2012.

Indeed, only nine England Caps have been won by Sunderland players since 1999. Only 21 England Caps for the Mackems in the last 50 years and eight of those 21 were picked up by Kevin Phillips.

The entire Sunderland history of 101 England Caps could be exceeded by their old mate Jordan Pickford in the near future, he has 94 England Caps whilst playing for Everton.

Intriguingly, Sunderland are a distant third when it comes to the north east clubs, as when it comes to England Caps it is now Newcastle United 347, Middlesbrough players 167 and then Sunderland on that total of 101.

#2000. Left out: High mileage Hammer’s injury sparks longer term fitness worries | West Ham News

There’ll be some relief amongst the West Ham medical staff at Rush Green tonight knowing that Manor Solomon was left out of Israel’s match altogether after the winger could not train owing to the pain of an ongoing injury.

However there will be concern that this same issue which dogged Solomon through September might yet prevent him playing his full part in the busy run up to Christmas  – with its demanding schedule of nine games in a little over a month.

Solomon came back from the last international break in September looking washed out, and in truth, his performances since have been a disappointment after his early season impact and man-of-the-match award.

Solomon – early season form has fallen away as his back injury has made itself known

There’s been a sneaking suspicion that Solomon has been playing with an injury -and this would seem to be confirmed by his being left out of his national side. In truth he probably should not even have travelled. According to Yahoo Sports:

“The winger missed out on the Israel squad completely for the 0-0 draw with Kosovo on Saturday.

Solomon had been suffering from back issues, and only partially trained on Wednesday.

He participated in the first session, before missing the second one and then tried to train on Friday.

However, Israeli boss Ran Ben-Shimon confirmed that he was in too much pain, and ultimately left him out of the contest.”

From a purely selfish club vs country perspective, West Ham could really do with the winger sitting out Israel’s next fixture against Austria on Tuesday evening.

Whilst Edvin Austbø has pulled ahead of Solomon in the pecking order, I shouldn’t wonder if Solomon’s back problems have been affecting him ever since he arrived at London Stadium and as the hours on the pitch have racked up, his high-energy output has nose dived.

#1999. Liverpool tipped for January squad boost absolutely no one wants

Harvey Elliott is reportedly set to be sent packing back home to Liverpool in January.

That’s the claim coming out of the regional Valencian outlet Las Provincias (via Sport Witness), with the midfielder having only picked up 152 La Liga minutes out of a possible 810 on offer.

After some concerns were expressed over the former Fulham academy graduate having arrived overweight in the Spanish top-flight, it seems the 23-year-old has been unable to make any headway at Mestalla.

It’s worth noting that a permanent decision has yet to be made by the club, despite a string of concerns, but Elliott very much appears to be in the last-chance saloon. In fact, as relayed by Sport Witness: “If he does not improve in the coming weeks, the loan agreement with Liverpool could be terminated. They state that ‘talks will be held’.”

Not a lot of time for the footballer to buck up his ideas and earn himself a place in the hearts of the Valencia fans and, importantly, the decision-makers at the outfit.

It’s not looking great for Harvey Elliott, it has to be said.

After basically being iced out of the Liverpool squad by former Reds head coach Andoni Iraola, the playmaker was shipped off to Unai Emery’s Aston Villa and only picked up 284 minutes of action.

Mind, there seemed to be a weird kind of power play going on between Liverpool and the Villans, with the Reds unwilling to pay a significant amount of cash to cut the loan short and Emery’s side being apparently fine with letting a young player rot on the bench to make a point.

Point made. And now Elliott’s future is paying for it.

We do want to state, unequivocally, that we believe in Harvey Elliott and his potential. It wasn’t a million years ago when we were watching him thriving as part of Jurgen Klopp’s deep squad in the German’s final season in charge in 2023/24. But that season is becoming increasingly distant, and it’s becoming increasingly difficult to imagine Elliott ever playing a significant role for Liverpool again in future.

We hope he can turn things around in Valencia. Because if our No.19 comes back to L4 in January, it’s not an eventuality that will suit the player or the club at this stage.

#1998. “Superb” international performance throws Scott Parker a curve ball | West Ham News

The international break has been full of surprises for West Ham‘s participants. Not all of them good. The humbling of Dinos Mavropanos Greece side by the seven goal Dutch. Tomas Soucek’s return to the Czech side marked by a late mistake. Manor Solomon’s complete exclusion from the Israel side.

Few, surely, would have expected the headlines this morning to be fêting one West Ham player who has been roundly condemned for his domestic form.

Mads Hermansen had conceded eleven goals – without making a save – in his last four appearances in the Championship and had one of the worst shot to saves ratio within the division.

On top form for Denmark – is it the man or is it his defence? Parker has a conundrum.

And yet, yesterday he almost single handedly kept out the Portugal attack as his Denmark national side trounced their opponents 4-1 with the Dane making eight saves.

Pretty much more than he’s managed in fifteen starts for West Ham, in one ninety minute spell when he was only beaten in added time. Labelled as ‘superb’ by his own club web site but as ‘sublime’ by one football.com, the Dane has thrown down the gauntlet (goal keeping gloves) to his critics and has thrown a selection curve ball for Scott Parker, with West Ham fans clamouring for the Danish shot stopper to be dropped in favour of the apparently unfit Alphonse Areola.

85% of West Ham fans, to be exact. Now that leaves Scott Parker with a real dilemma. Fortunately Hermansen will have another outing on Tuesday against Norway before returning to Rush Green, giving the West Ham coach more food for thought.

Several West Ham accounts on line overnight have leapt to the conclusion that Hermansen’s West Ham form must be completely down to the woeful defence ahead of him. They may have a point. It is quite possible also that Hermansen has the confidence to perform better on the international stage in front of a group of supporters who aren’t on his back for 90 minutes. That may also be true.

#1996. Chaos appears to be following one West Ham want away as upheaval continues

There’s been another twist in the chaotic career of one of West Ham’s standout signings of the Tim Steidten era.

It would be fair to say that Jean Clair Todibo was largely unknown to Hammers fans when Tim Stediten whisked the former Barca defender to east London in his private jet for a VIP welcome in the summer of 2024.

Sadly its would also be fair to say that the defender has been part of a chaotic two and a half years during which he’s seen three West Ham managers – and fallen out with all of them – and declared himself unwilling to play for the club again.

Todibo – dressing room chaos never seems far away

Chaos appears to have followed Todibo to France when West Ham finally – gratefully – found a loan destination for their unhappy defender in the summer as Todibo was sent to Lens owing to his desire (apparently) to work with manager Dino Toppmoller.

No sooner had the wayward West Ham defender landed than Toppmoller was fired – and his successor Yannick Cahuzac fared little better, lasting just two months.

Todibo is surely the only player in the Lens dressing room who will have played under six managers in side three years, as his new head coach is revealed as Didier Digard.

Scott Parker can’t have missed the fact that Todibo is due to return to east London at the end of the season – putting the defender on course to test Parker’s own managerial credentials when his loan ends next May. And few West Ham fans will welcome him back after his turbulent and truculent career in Claret and Blue.

#1994. Lamine Yamal outclassed by Lewis Hall, again

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Lewis Hall outclassed Lamine Yamal in Madrid.

The match ending Spain 2 England 3 but that only tells a very small part of the story.

England by a huge distance the better team and going 3-0 up in less than an hour, it should have been more.

Spain massively got away with one as moments of madness from Jarell Quansah, Elliot Anderson and Anthony Gordon, threatened to destroy what had been a supreme team performance.

With England so much on top, their individual errors in a 12 minute second half spell directly led to the two undeserved Spanish goals and Thomas Tuchel’s team having to play the final 30 or so minutes a man down.

Somebody who didn’t put a foot wrong was Lewis Hall.

We have to now pay tribute and give our thanks to those in the media who have now suddenly ‘discovered’ the brilliant 22-year-old.

I wonder what lifelong Newcastle United fan Lewis Hall has been up to these last few years…?

Lamine Yamal had played in 32 competitive matches for Spain, where they had won 27 of them, drawing five and losing none.

Then the winger ran into Lewis Hall, again.

Lamine Yamal losing in his 33rd competitive appearance for Spain, his first ever.

The only surprise about this Lamine Yamal v Lewis Hall contest was that anybody should be surprised.

It was only in March this year that the pair were up against each other when Newcastle United hosted Barcelona at St James’ Park, Lewis Hall up against Lamine Yamal.

Lamine Yamal scored a fortunate late equaliser from the penalty spot, however, there was no doubt about who won this duel of top class winger and elite lifelong Newcastle United fan.

Barcelona star man Lamine Yamal wasn’t able to dribble past Lewis Hall even once in the 90+ minutes. Whilst the United defender was superb going forward, creating five chances, the most created by any player on the pitch.

On top of all of that, the appalling referee failed to book Lamine Yamal for a cynical foul on Lewis Hall, after yet again the NUFC player got the better of him. A yellow card which would have been Yamal’s third in the competition and seen him suspended for the second leg.

Last night in Madrid was very reminiscent of St James’ Park in March, the only joy Lamine Yamal got was when he was marked by somebody else out wide, or when he came inside to get away from Lewis Hall. Plus of course those two awful errors from Quansah and Gordon that led to the Spanish goals.

It was also amusing to see once again last night, what happens when things go against a young prima donna such as Lamine Yamal. His diving was so impressive and his petulance was a joy to see as he reacted to Hall and England’s dominance with fouls of his own as things weren’t going his and Spain’s way.

#1993. Championship data highlights exactly what West Ham’s midfield is still missing

A fascinating piece of Championship analysis from Loft Insights on X may provide an uncomfortable reminder of where West Ham’s midfield falls short.

The graphic plots central midfielders based on two key metrics: line-breaking passes per 90 minutes and ball-winning actions per 90 minutes. Put simply, it measures which players are able to progress the ball through opposition lines while also contributing defensively.

The most interesting takeaway for me was not necessarily which players stand out, but where West Ham’s own midfield profiles sit on the chart.

The Championship’s elite midfielders increasingly occupy the top-right quadrant, combining progression and defensive intensity. That is why the chart identifies Norwich City’s Kenny McLean as one of the Championship’s most complete midfielders, posting outstanding line-breaking numbers while maintaining strong defensive output, despite only featuring for ten games out of fifteen due to an ankle injury.

Meanwhile, Portsmouth’s Ebou Adams is highlighted as a “defensive monster”, producing exceptional ball-winning statistics while still offering significant progression. Sheffield United’s Kalvin Phillips (yes the same player that flopped on loan at West Ham!), Queens Park Rangers’ Jonathan Varane and Norwich’s Jacob Wright also occupy impressive positions, demonstrating the ability to impact both sides of the game.

Mohamadou Kanté is viewed as a dynamic ball-carrying midfielder with strong physical attributes, but his game is built more around energy and transition play than elite progression metrics. Arne Engels offers technical quality and creativity, yet is generally more comfortable operating higher up the pitch than acting as a defensive controller.

The data is only based on players who have played an average of 540 mins so one omission is Tomas Souček, whose strengths have always been obvious. The Czech international on paper would arguably be the Championships most effective midfield goalscorer (3 in 7 appearances so far) and I’d expect him to feature highly for aerial presence. However, if plotted on a graph measuring line-breaking passes and ball-winning volume, he would likely owe more to his physicality and attacking threat than his ability to dictate possession through midfield.

That perhaps explains why West Ham can sometimes appear disconnected between defence and attack.

Too often there is a reliance on direct balls into attacking areas rather than building through the centre of the pitch. Equally, when possession is lost, the midfield does not always possess the combination of mobility and defensive output needed to regain control quickly.

West Ham arguably have midfielders who can create and win duels. What they appear to lack is a genuine “two-way” midfielder capable of consistently ranking highly in both categories.

That was precisely what Declan Rice offered during his time at the club. His ability to recover possession and immediately progress the ball remains incredibly difficult to replace.

The reality is Rice was never truly replaced, although finding a like-for-like successor was always going to be a near-impossible task

Former West Ham midfielder James Ward-Prowse’s position on the chart is also interesting. A casualty of Nuno’s reign, he ranks among the highest players for line-breaking passes but has one of the lowest ball-winning outputs. Ward-Prowse excels at progressing possession but offers relatively little defensive contribution compared to the league’s most complete midfielders.

Above all the data serves as a reminder that Koppen’s recruitment and Parker’s existing choices for midfield should focus less on individual statistics and more on complete profiles.

Because the numbers suggest that is where Championship matches are increasingly won.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

I think there is nothing wrong with the Midfield. There is just a problem with the short pass mentality. The day of playing short passes across midfield are over in English football. You need decent long passes with good trapping and decent positive movement. How many of West Ham’s passes are square ball or back passes ? Far to many. Particularly back passes are all to often caught on to giving away needless goals. Walker-Peters is a really good example. Having moved forward beating someone, he then passes back in midfield, or worst still carries the ball backwards towards midfield or defence. Play positively, avoid back passes, learn to pass well and trap well and you have a very good midfield. Orford, Kante and other young players are far better at doing this, than the older players.

#1992. Ian Rush calls out bizarre Alexander Isak criticism after electric start rivals Haaland

Ian Rush has disagreed with the common consensus about Alexander Isak this season.

The Swedish international has been accused, at various times this season, of not being actively involved during Liverpool games.

As Rush was at pains to point out, the former Newcastle United hitman is scoring goals this season. Enough, at any rate, to put him in early contention with Manchester City’s Erling Haaland for the golden boot, with seven Premier League goals registered to the Norwegian’s nine – and in one fewer game to boot.

“People say that Isak isn’t getting involved much but he’s scoring goals and that’s all that matters. The hardest thing in football is to score a goal and he’s only second to (Erling) Haaland,” the Liverpool legend told BBC Sport.

It seems that no matter what the 27-year-old does in the famous red shirt, someone will have something negative to say about his performances.

But the fact remains that Isak is managing to get on the scoresheet with some degree of frequency as part of a frontline that is far from cohesive at this stage.

Can you imagine how many times he’ll be finding the back of the net once he finds a collective rhythm alongside Cody Gakpo and Bradley Barcola?

One may reasonably be inclined to think that critics have forgotten how Isak had the debut season from hell at Liverpool following his move from Newcastle in the summer.

The forward managed only 1,032 minutes across all competitions in Arne Slot’s final season in charge, between adductor issues and a broken fibula. 1,032 minutes, four goals and one assist. In 2026/27, the Swede has already racked up eight goals and an assist in 899 minutes of action (across all competitions).

Far easier for Alexander Isak to build fluency when he’s spending a lot more time on the pitch early in the season and stringing a series of starts together from one game to the next.

David Martin’s West Ham career was short but never-to-be-forgotten

#1990. For Newcastle United these are now the steps that matter

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

There are Newcastle United seasons that announce themselves with the flourish of a fanfare, and there are seasons that arrive more quietly, almost tentatively, as if testing the ground beneath their feet.

This one, for Newcastle United, belongs firmly to the latter category.

Ten Premier League matches into the 2026-27 campaign, the Magpies sit in twelfth place with twelve points. Three victories, three draws, four defeats.

The numbers are neither catastrophic nor comforting. They are, instead, the arithmetic of transition.

After years of ascent under Eddie Howe—punctuated by European nights and the rare, precious taste of silverware—the club has entered a deliberate, if painful, period of reconstruction. Key figures have departed. Younger, less seasoned players have arrived. And into this unsettled landscape has stepped Matthias Jaissle, a thoughtful German coach still learning the particular cadences of the Premier League. Let’s pray he is precocious!

The style he favors—“vertical football”—is direct, urgent, and ambitious. Yet in these early weeks it has often looked unfinished, like a promising manuscript that still requires careful editing. Attacks break down before they fully form. The midfield sometimes lacks the necessary ballast. Set-pieces, once a source of both goals and defensive security, have lost their edge. Chance creation has been modest. The underlying numbers suggest a side that is still searching for its rhythm.

I would argue that the back half of last season under Eddie Howe, and with the “superstars” who moved on to their perceived “bigger” clubs, the performances were no better. I flew 3,500 miles to attend the Bournemouth match – at great expense may I add – to witness the worst Newcastle United performance in my near 50 years of following the club. The rot started last season (and I would venture to say in the summer of 2025).

None of this should surprise those who have followed the club’s longer story. Newcastle has always been a place where ambition and constraint exist in uneasy conversation. The Saudi ownership brought resources and expectation, but the financial rules of the modern game impose their own discipline, that I wish would be challenged in court as anti-competitive.

The past 2026 summer window reflected that reality: significant investment, yes, but also the departure of established leaders (good riddance to the rats!) and the calculated gamble on potential rather than proven readiness.

Still, there are concrete steps available this season—practical, unglamorous steps that can steady the ship without pretending the rebuild is already complete.

Matthias Jaissle must first allow himself the freedom of pragmatism. The purest version of his vertical approach has, at times, left the team exposed and the attack under-supplied. A measured adjustment—greater control in build-up when the high press is broken, tighter rest defence, a clearer structure for the attacking midfielder—need not abandon the philosophy. It would simply make it sustainable. Restoring set-piece competence would be another quiet victory. These are matters of coaching detail, not revolution.

The Newcastle United squad itself still holds untapped value. Joelinton’s physical presence and ball-winning capacity remain essential once fully available, but we have a young gem in Sean Steur who, whilst not as physically imposing as Big Joe, is poised, creative, and doesn’t mind sticking a foot in. Dan Burn’s leadership and aerial strength can stabilise both ends of the pitch. The younger summer arrivals require patience but also clear pathways and honest assessment. A stable selection, built around those who are ready rather than those who might be ready later, would help establish the consistency that has been missing.

Then there is January. The winter window is rarely the stage for transformative spending at a club managing financial ratios carefully. Yet it can be the stage for precise, intelligent reinforcement. The most glaring absence is a natural number ten—a player capable of receiving between the lines, linking midfield to attack, and providing the creative spark that current options have not consistently delivered.

One name that has already circulated is Bilal El Khannouss of Stuttgart. The Morocco international attacking midfielder was reportedly considered during the summer and is claimed to be available for a fee in the region of no more than£40 million, a figure that may prove more attainable than many alternatives. His profile—technical, progressive, comfortable in the half-spaces—aligns with what Jaissle appears to seek. Other options will be examined, of course. The market rarely offers perfect solutions in January. But the principle is clear: a ready-made creator who can accelerate the adaptation of the system would be more valuable than another project requiring time the club may not fully possess this season. Contract situations must also be addressed with clarity. Players entering the final year of their deals create both risk and opportunity. Selling at the right moment, rather than losing assets for nothing, can fund the necessary additions while maintaining squad balance.

None of this guarantees a return by Newcastle United to the higher reaches of the table overnight. That would be unrealistic. What it can provide is direction—a sense that the transition is being managed with purpose rather than simply endured. A top-half finish, or even a secure mid-table campaign accompanied by improved underlying performance, would represent genuine progress under the circumstances.

Football clubs, like the cities they represent, are defined as much by how they navigate difficulty as by how they celebrate success. Newcastle has known both extremes in recent years. The current chapter is quieter, more complicated, and less cinematic than the ones that preceded it. Yet it is no less consequential.

The work of improvement rarely arrives with trumpets. It arrives in adjustments of shape, in the careful acquisition of the right player at the right moment, and in the daily insistence that potential must eventually become performance. For Newcastle United this season, those are the steps that matter. The rest will follow, or it will not. But the path, at least, can be chosen with intention.

Six weeks left before Christmas means a hectic Championship period with West Ham United facing nine games before the transfer window opens once again: It hardly seems a month since the summer window closed.

West Ham have, according to journo Alan Nixon, as we covered earlier, made their top transfer targets clear: A left back and a striker. The poor performance of the frontline trio at east London – with Joel Piroe the best of a bad bunch – has left Scott Parker pushing for a new frontman in January.

Pablo Felipe- monumental waste of money who’s impact has been minimal

#1988. Palmer and Rogers complete 12-minute rescue mission to save Chelsea

Xabi Alonso needed the cavalry – and referee Jarred Gillett – to stop Chelsea making a quick exit from the Carabao Cup and, boy, did they come up trumps for him.

Chelsea had looked to be heading out of the competition shortly after half-time, but, in Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, Alonso has a cheat code that is capable of masking even the worst defending.

Alonso’s side have shared 26 goals in the five games they have played this season. It has certainly been an entertaining start by Chelsea’s latest manager.

Palmer, Rogers and Pedro Neto stepped off the substitutes’ bench to complete a stunning rescue mission against Leeds United. Palmer scored twice, Neto once and Rogers helped himself to at least a hat-trick of assists. He claimed it was four, but the record books may say three.

When it was announced Palmer had been awarded the player of the match, Rogers responded by saying: “Mate, I got four assists. I can’t believe that! That’s mental. He scored a pen!”

"Mate, I got four assists!" "That is criminal!" Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer arguing over the POTM award! 🤣 pic.twitter.com/X2PkPnSGDk

Chelsea had looked down and out, when, just three minutes after Alonso’s quadruple half-time change, Leeds doubled their lead. But four goals in an incredible 12-minute spell turned the tie on its head and it was Alonso’s substitutes who Chelsea had to thank.

Palmer, with some help from Gillett, was the first to come to the home side’s rescue. Four minutes after Brenden Aaronson had put Leeds 2-0 up, Gillett pointed to the penalty spot after Daniel James had stood on the foot of Pep Chavarría.

It looked like a harsh decision on Leeds and proved to be almost as big of a game-changer as Alonso’s substitutions. Palmer stepped up to score the resulting penalty.

Cole Palmer pulls one back for Chelsea from the spot! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/BUv6h1wTPQ

“Nobody in the stadium, not one player was asking for a penalty and he gave the penalty,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, said. “All of a sudden their players came into the game. The momentum was on their side. Situations can change the whole momentum of the game.”

Stamford Bridge sensed a comeback and in the 55th minute, Rogers nudged the ball into the path of Palmer who produced a brilliant curling finish to beat Michael Zetterer, the Leeds goalkeeper.

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

Reece James then went close, before Neto completed the turnaround on the hour mark. Palmer found Rogers, who in turn picked out Neto and he sent Stamford Bridge wild by sending his shot into the corner of the net.

"This is a comeback of comebacks!" Pedro Neto scores and Chelsea have turned it around eleven minutes after going 2-0 down! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/FTPuWcFqEX

As Farke waited to make a quadruple substitution of his own, Danny Welbeck got in on the act by collecting the ball from Rogers, spinning and scoring.

Class from Danny Welbeck 😤 pic.twitter.com/FUFKxlzXDz

That should have been that and the atmosphere could not have been more different from half-time, when Chelsea fans had booed off their side after watching them fall a goal behind.

Reggie Watson, Chelsea’s 16-year-old debutant, Malo Gusto, Estêvão Willian and Jamie Gittens were hooked at half-time by Alonso, who said: “For sure, I take responsibility for all of them. No player to blame. It’s the decisions that we took.

“I know that probably I haven’t taken the right decisions for them to show their best level. It’s something that I will analyse and learn from. So it’s my responsibility and we had to make decisions at half-time. And we have seen another second half with another quality.”

Goalkeeper Mike Penders was one of the nine changes made by Alonso. He produced a superb double-save to first keep out Aaronson and then recover to tip Tarik Muharemovic’s header out from the corner.

Conor Coady was impressed with that Mike Penders double save in the first half 👏 pic.twitter.com/6NJqFDvnzk

But the Belgian flapped at the corner, which gave Harry Wilson a second chance to get his delivery right. And he did just that by finding Muharemovic at the back post to head the ball into the net.

Valentín Barco survived Alonso’s changes, but was partly at fault for Leeds’s second goal just after the break. He lost the ball and Ethan Ampadu galloped away from Rogers before crossing. Lukas Nmecha got the slightest of touches and Aaronsen smashed the ball into the net.

"Chelsea cut apart AGAIN !" Brenden Aaronson makes it 2-0 to Leeds 🔥 pic.twitter.com/LlJNpqXHav

The substitutes then took over, as Chelsea shocked the visitors before Leeds substitute Dominic Calvert-Lewin gave his team hope by reducing the deficit with 15 minutes remaining.

Any thoughts of a Leeds comeback were quickly erased, however, as Barco netted his first Chelsea goal from a Rogers pass, which may have taken a slight touch to deny him a fourth assist in the record books. Welbeck added a sixth in time added on.

Valentín Barco gets Chelsea a FIFTH! 🫨 pic.twitter.com/XnhgvhBpL9

On the defeat by Chelsea, Farke said: “The referee had the idea to give a penalty. No one in the stadium was asking for it, no one of their players was asking for it, but he spotted a situation where he thought he would give a penalty.

“All of a sudden they scored the goal, then their players came into the game at half-time, the whole stadium after being relatively quiet for 60 minutes they of course were there then. The momentum was all of a sudden on their side. In football small situations can change the whole momentum of a game and this happened.”

"100% I meant it!" 😅Morgan Rogers says he is really enjoying his football after he helped Chelsea beat Leeds 6-3 in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/7uUQb6eIla

Here’s a reminder of the assist in question. Did Rogers mean it? Let us know in the comments beneath this live blog...

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

"Mate, I got four assists!" "That is criminal!" Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer arguing over the POTM award! 🤣 pic.twitter.com/X2PkPnSGDk

On the message from the manager at half-time, Palmer told Sky Sports: “Just up the intensity, play a bit more, become more alive because I think the first half was flat, everyone agreed in the changing room, so we stepped up.

Asked whether Alonso’s message was delivered calmly, he said: “At the start, but then he got a bit angry. But it was alright.”

On Chelsea’s half-time changes, Conor Coady said on Sky Sports: “I think the credit goes down to [Alonso]. He made a bit of a statement by doing that at half-time. Four subs is a lot to do at half-time but it was needed. Listen, we said about the first half that it was kind of like the players hadn’t played with each other, and then the big guns came on... They were electric at times.”

A crazy match which was decided by Chelsea’s superb substitutes. Alonso took action at half-time and was rewarded with six goals in a madcap second half. Palmer hauled Chelsea back into the game, Rogers collected a handful of assists and Neto scored the go-ahead goal. You wonder what this match will do for the likes of Estevao and Gittens, though.

Chelsea 6 Leeds United 3 (Welbeck) Pure reflexes from Welbeck, who diverts Barco’s wild effort beyond Zetterer.

Palmer has the hat-trick ball on his mind and attempts an audacious chip but just gets his angles wrong. Any guesses who laid on the chance? Rogers. Of course.

Fans in the away end have resolved they have seen enough and are now heading towards the exits. Stach attempts to launch a counter but his raking cross-field ball is far too heavy.

Rogers drifts out to the left and wins Chelsea a valuable corner. James walks over to take it to rapturous applause from supporters there.

Leeds look to break but Wilson mistimes his run and is caught offside.

There will be six minutes of time added on.

Chance! Okafor darts inside of Neto and spins in a teasing ball to the back post but neither Calvert-Lewin nor Tanaka are able to reach it.

Shouts for a Leeds penalty fail to pique the interest of referee Gillett. Gudmundsson was felled on the left of the box but the contact looked minimal.

A tap on Barco’s head from Wilson provokes some histrionics from the Argentine but Jarred Gillett calms all parties down.

Leeds are still pushing. Stach’s effort from eight yards out is closed down before Tanaka’s strike from the edge of the box is smothered by James.

Alonso goes into the book, apparently for straying too far outside of his technical area.

Chelsea 5 Leeds United 3 (Barco) Rogers lays on his fourth assist of the match, driving towards the byline before flashing a searching ball across the face of goal which Barco spears past Zetterer at the far post. That should be that, right?

Valentín Barco gets Chelsea a FIFTH! 🫨 pic.twitter.com/XnhgvhBpL9

Gudmundsson replaces debutant Bard down Leeds’ left.

Chelsea 4 Leeds United 3 (Calvert-Lewin) Game back on? Okafor is afforded far too much space down the left by a tiring Chelsea back line and his cross finds Calvert-Lewin who plants the ball past Penders to reduce the deficit to just one goal. What a tie this has turned into!

Leeds win a corner, which falls to Stach on the edge of the box but his effort is charged down.

It will be a source of acute anguish for Farke that Chelsea’s fourth goal came before he could make his four changes: Stach, Calvert-Lewin, Tanaka and Okafor eventually replace James, Nmecha, Longstaff and Aaronson. Conversely, it should be to Alonso’s credit that he took action early - his substitutes have decided this tie.

Chelsea 4 Leeds United 2 (Welbeck) Rogers gallops on to a simple ball down the right channel and his cutback (towards Palmer) is picked up by Welbeck who spins before firing beyond Zetterer, leaving three Leeds defenders sprawled in front of him. He cares not, and absorbs the love of the crowd in the near corner.

Class from Danny Welbeck 😤 pic.twitter.com/FUFKxlzXDz

Palmer goes close after having found a yard of space on the edge of the box. His strike spears through a thicket of limbs in Leeds’ box but Zetterer pulls off a strong save to deny the Englishman a quickfire hat-trick.

Chelsea 3 Leeds United 2 (Neto) Just 11 minutes after going 2-0 down, Chelsea find themselves ahead. Palmer threads a through-ball through the middle for Rogers, who slides in front of his marker to an open Neto who sweeps the ball beyond Zetterer. Leeds punished for leaving themselves two vs two at the back there.

"This is a comeback of comebacks!" Pedro Neto scores and Chelsea have turned it around eleven minutes after going 2-0 down! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/FTPuWcFqEX

Chelsea have got their tails up and Palmer almost lays on a go-ahead goal but James cannot turn in his cross from the left.

Chelsea 2 Leeds United 2 (Palmer) Wow! Palmer has turned this game on its head. And it’s so, so simple. Acheampong’s throw-in is knocked down by Rogers into the path of Palmer who works in from the right, passing the ball around a Leeds defender and past a rooted Zetterer.

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

Chelsea 1 Leeds United 2 (Palmer) Palmer makes no mistake. He goes right, and while Zetterer guesses the right way he cannot get there and Chelsea are back in business.

Cole Palmer pulls one back for Chelsea from the spot! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/BUv6h1wTPQ

Chavarria is caught by James in the box and the referee points to the spot. That came from nowhere.

Chelsea 0 Leeds United 2 (Aaronson) Amapadu deserves so much credit here. He steals the ball from Barco high, bursts beyond Rogers on the right and while Nmecha cannot turn in his cutback, Aaronson arrives late to stroke the ball past Penders and double Leeds’ lead.

"Chelsea cut apart AGAIN !" Brenden Aaronson makes it 2-0 to Leeds 🔥 pic.twitter.com/LlJNpqXHav

Alonso resolves he has seen enough and rings the changes at the interval. Palmer, Rogers, James and Neto enter the fray in place of Estevao, Watson, Gittens and Gusto.

Big cheers from the Chelsea fans at half-time, as Cole Palmer, Pedro Neto, Morgan Rogers and Reece James have all come on to warm up and are stripped off ready to play. Alonso is sending on the cavalry.

The delayed kick-off has knocked us out of kilter with tonight’s Champions League matches, but here are the live scores:

Liverpool 2 Atletico Madrid 1Paris St-Germain 4 Slovan 0Napoli 0 Arsenal 0Sporting CP 1 Galatasaray 1

Boos at half-time from the Chelsea fans. Their team were pretty awful, but booing so early in the season. Really?

There is only one minute of time added on and Watson earns himself a booking for a late challenge on Wilson before the half-time whistle is blown. It will be interesting to see how long Alonso waits before turning to his bench.

Justin, James and Wilson have got a lot of joy down Leeds’ right, rotating in Chavarria’s orbit. It has been difficult for Chelsea to pin them down and Gittens’ attacking threat has been blunted as he attempts to track their movements.

Better from Chelsea. Watson does well to regain possession high and Estevao takes over, darting towards the by-line. His cutback is directed towards Welbeck but he is beaten to the ball by a Leeds toe and it is played behind for a corner which comes to nothing.

Chelsea are really struggling to build up a head of steam, with individual mistakes proving costly.

Gittens and Estevao both end up on the left and the former works infield before firing a shot at Zetterer which the German parries behind for a corner. Perhaps Chelsea’s most dangerous moment of the half.

The corner is played short with the ball eventually falling to Barco on the edge of the box but his mis-hit effort trickles wide.

Gittens rescues an overhit Acheampong cross and finds Barco on the edge of the box, but the Argentine’s effort is charged down. Leeds spring a counter and their sweeping move up field earns them a corner.

Wilson floats another delivery to the back post to Muharemovic, but he cannot replicate his earlier goal.

Farke will be delighted with what he has seen so far. It is all well and good Chelsea allowing Leeds the ball, but they have to break incisively when openings arise, and they have not done that.

Big chance for Leeds! James bursts down the right and the Welsh winger dinks in a cross to the far post which Justin cannot get past Acheampong, but while Longstaff is first to the second ball, he can only sky the shot over the bar.

Leeds’ goal has stirred something inside them and they look motivated to score a second. Ampadu launches a long throw from the left which ricochets off a couple of players before rolling out for a Chelsea goal-kick.

Chelsea 0 Leeds United 1 (Muharemovic) Set-pieces have been a massive feature of Leeds’ game this season and here they take the lead with the simplest of corner routines. Wilson floats the ball to the back post where Muharemovic is waiting, unmarked, and he loops a header over Penders into the net. Such a shame for the Chelsea keeper as he had just pulled off a stunning double-save.

"The set-piece routine does it again!" Tarik Muharemović puts Leeds in front against Chelsea! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/UxeJ3xgL56

Barco slips on the far side and in doing so concedes a corner rather comically, to the delight of the travelling supporters. The delivery is met by Lacroix and Leeds are unable to create anything from the second phase of the set-piece.

There is an intriguing duel developing down Chelsea’s right as Bard looks to contain Estevao. The French wing-back has done a decent job so far.

Estevao attempts to free himself of Bard’s clutches and drifts inside, Chavarria then almost picks him out with a cross from the left but Leeds just about clear their lines.

Justin plays in a cultured through-ball from a wide-right position to James but Chavarria does well to snuff it out. Leeds are making the pitch as big as possible and spaces are beginning to open up as they did at Fulham on the opening weekend.

Although Penders’ shot-stopping has not yet been tested, he has shown some nifty footwork, sweeping up any loose balls that make it past Chelsea’s back three/five.

Big chance! Chelsea spring a surprise attack as Chavarria sets Gittens away down the left. He works the ball infield to Welbeck who lays on a great chance for Estevao but Justin darts back to take the ball off the Brazilian’s toes. A brilliant piece of last-ditch defending.

Gittens gets a shot away, a tame effort straight at Zetterer from 22 yards out as he cuts in from the left. The correct intent, though.

Leeds look to circulate the ball across their back line. As mentioned pre-match, Chelsea will not mind letting their opponents get on the ball as they set out-of-possession traps. Aaronson eventually dribbles off the pitch on the far side.

Chelsea’s Argentine midfielder, Valentin Barco, is being booed by the Leeds fans every time he touches the ball. Barco will already be used to getting that treatment, as it has even happened to him while he’s been a substitute this season.

In other news, there’s a real Borussia Dortmund vibe to this Leeds away kit.

Leeds supporters boo Argentina World Cup squad member Barco’s every touch, and another Leeds foul, this time Justin on Gittens, prompts a second Chelsea free-kick.

A couple of early touches for Watson who plays a neat pass around the corner. Ampadu then lands a late tackle on Lacroix and Chelsea earn a free-kick in their own half.

Although there are still some empty seats, we are finally under way. Chelsea in their customary all blue, kicking from right to left. Leeds in their yellow away strip.

Chelsea and Leeds emerge from the tunnel, led out by Colwill and former Chelsea defender Ampadu. Here’s a reminder of the teams in full:

Chelsea Penders; Gusto, Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill, Chavarria; Watson, Barco; Estevao, Gittens; Welbeck

Substitutes Martinez, Hato, Fofana, James, Neto, Palmer, Quenda, Rogers, Pedro

Leeds United Zetterer; Justin, Bijol, Muharemovic; James, Ampadu, Longstaff, Bard; Wilson, Aaronson; Nmecha

Substitutes Trafford, Gudmundsson, Elvedi, Bogle, Tanaka, Stach, Okafor, Calvert-Lewin, Bahoya

Daniel Farke believes Leeds can go far in the Carabao Cup this year 💪 pic.twitter.com/26ueAAUHoZ

On the Brazilian winger’s opportunity tonight, Hasselbaink said on Sky Sports: “He has to find his place. This is his opportunity... It’s not really an out-and-out left-wing [position] or a No 10 as he can play, but [with] good players it doesn’t matter where you put them on the pitch. He will find his spaces and he will be direct as he was when he came in against Arsenal. He is going to play for his place because he wants to play week-in, week-out.”

"He deserves to be there because of what he has shown" Xabi Alonso speaks about Reggie Watson with the 16-year-old set to make his Chelsea debut in their Carabao Cup game against Leeds 🌟 pic.twitter.com/AAn4Av3iEh

Tfl has closed South Kensington station after a “customer incident” meaning parts of the District Line have closed. The decision was then made to delay the match to give supporters more time to get to the stadium.

Reggie Watson will become the fourth youngest player, aged 16, in Chelsea’s history. But he will have to wait a little bit longer for his debut as kick-off has been delayed by 15 minutes to 8.15pm.

There will be a 15 minute delay to kick-off for our Carabao Cup third round tie with Leeds United tonight. The match will now begin at 20:15 BST. pic.twitter.com/MdDXpxgW09

LeedsAug 22: Nottingham Forest 0 Leeds 1Aug 25: Nottingham Forest 0 Leeds 2Aug 30: Leeds 1 Brentford 1Sep 5: Brighton 1 Leeds 1

As recently as March, a giant mural of Estêvão Willian appeared on the side of a building outside Stamford Bridge as the teenager threatened to become Chelsea’s number one poster boy.

He may no longer hold top billing outside the club, following a summer in which Chelsea spent a club-record £117m on Morgan Rogers to complete a fearsome front three alongside Cole Palmer and João Pedro.

A giant mural of the Brazilian teenager appeared on the side of a building close to Stamford Bridge in March.

But inside Stamford Bridge, nothing has changed. Estêvão remains one of Chelsea’s star boys and is part of an “untouchable” group of players that also includes Palmer, Rogers and Pedro. Sources believe Estêvão is a player the club will look at rewarding with an improved contract in the coming months.

Having already earned his Chelsea “untouchable” status, the next challenge for the 19-year-old winger – once nicknamed “Messinho” – is to make himself undroppable.

Estêvão may not be a perfect fit for Xabi Alonso’s three-at-the-back formation that features two 10s – Palmer and Rogers – behind a striker. But the boy from Brazil is certainly not being squeezed out and Chelsea’s manager has spoken of the need to be flexible.

Chelsea Penders; Gusto, Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill, Chavarria; Watson, Barco; Estevao, Gittens; Welbeck

Substitutes Martinez, Hato, Fofana, James, Neto, Palmer, Quenda, Rogers, Pedro

Leeds United Zetterer; Justin, Bijol, Muharemovic; James, Ampadu, Longstaff, Bard; Wilson, Aaronson; Nmecha

Substitutes Trafford, Gudmundsson, Elvedi, Bogle, Tanaka, Stach, Okafor, Calvert-Lewin, Bahoya

Much has been made of Chelsea’s willingness to let the opposition have the ball under Xabi Alonso, but tonight they will likely be forced to dictate proceedings. In Leeds, they face one of only two sides who have completed fewer passes than them in the Premier League.

1. Ian Hamilton in 1967: 16 years, four months and 15 days2. Kingsley Whiffen in 1967: 16 years, five months and six days3. Reggie Walsh in 2025: 16 years, six months and 11 days4. Reggie Watson in 2026: 16 years, seven months and 14 days5. Tommy Langley in 1974: 16 years, nine months and one day

Asked how he will approach the Carabao Cup this season, Daniel Farke said: “We’ll try to win it. That’s the quickest way to Europe and to some glory. Of course knowing that the Premier League will always have the priority and knowing that we are as successful as possible there, especially to reach our first goal to establish ourselves [at] this level.

“We are not the favourites to win the Carabao Cup, we know this. Challenging, difficult games, but of course we travel to London in order to go through in the next round without doing anything stupid at this stage of the campaign because you also have to rotate a bit more and integrate a few new players. Nevertheless, we want to be at our best and anyhow possible we also want to go through to the next round.”

Tonight represents an opportunity for 16-year-old Reggie Watson to announce himself at senior level. The central-midfielder caught Alonso’s eye during pre-season when the Spaniard said of him: “Reggie Watson, a great midfielder. He thinks, he’s very collective, he’s very generous on the effort, intelligent with the ball”.

“For his age, I’m really impressed with him.”

Dan James passes a late fitness test to make Daniel Farke’s starting XI.

📋 Tonight's Starting XI pic.twitter.com/MQKQtGZm8c

Reggie Watson, 16, son of former Wigan midfielder Ben (of 2013 FA Cup final fame), makes his full Chelsea debut and becomes the club’s fourth youngest player. Estevao, Jamie Gittens and Danny Welbeck replace Alonso’s thrilling forward three, who are on the bench.

Chelsea XI Penders; Gusto, Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill, Chavarria; Watson, Barco; Estevao, Gittens; Welbeck

Your Blues to face Leeds United in the #CarabaoCup! #CFC pic.twitter.com/636SOiUXVB

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of tonight’s Carabao Cup third-round tie between Chelsea and Leeds United. This is a rematch of last season’s FA Cup semi-final which Chelsea edged by a single Enzo Fernández goal, but plenty has changed since then. Xabi Alonso has taken over the reins at Stamford Bridge and made a promising start, reeling off three wins before losing to Arsenal in an absorbing contest last Sunday. Chelsea are not involved in European competition this season, so the domestic cups represent an avenue to silverware, as well as an opportunity to tinker.

In Alonso’s way, though, stands a Leeds team whose manager, Daniel Farke, told the media on Tuesday that his side are aiming to win the Carabao Cup. Farke has overseen an impressive run of form, having lost only two of their previous 16 competitive matches in a stretch that extends back to March. Two wins at Nottingham Forest preceded draws against Brentford and Brighton to keep Leeds undefeated this term. Farke has suggested he will rotate in west London to “integrate new players” having brought in seven new recruits during the summer.

If Leeds are to reach the next round, they must reverse a heavily one-sided head-to-head record against their hosts, who have won each of their past 10 cup meetings (three in the League Cup, seven in the FA Cup). In fact, Chelsea have lost at this stage of the competition just once in the past 15 years, and that was against Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City four seasons ago.

Alonso broke up the exhilarating “JP Morgan” band (João Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers) for Chelsea’s victory over Luton Town in the previous round, handing starts to Danny Welbeck and Estêvão. Players such as Jamie Gittens and Geovany Quenda are also waiting in the wings and may get chances to impress tonight. Mike Penders could also be in line for a start between the sticks.

On Thursday (16 November 2026), Crystal Palace sacked Pierre Sage.

The Selhurst Park club with official announcement on that Thursday afternoon.

Crystal Palace only though the second Premier League club to sack their manager during this 2026-27 season, as Manchester United beat them by a couple of hours by dismissing Michael Carrick.

We have since seen Man U announce Mauricio Pochettino as their new manager and now Crystal Palace set to name their replacement.

Monday has seen Sky Sports reveal that their information is that Crystal Palace ‘have agreed terms in principle’ with Thomas Frank.

This has been backed up by the likes of The Athletic, who report that Crystal Palace are finalising the deal and getting things in place whereby Frank’s preferred backroom team will also come into Selhurst Park.

Thomas Frank did a brilliant job for years at Brentford before becoming yet another manager to fail at Tottenham.

He will head into Crystal Palace to find a team rock bottom of the Premier League with only seven points after ten matches.

International breaks are always a popular time for sacking Premier League managers with a bit of time to appoint a replacement before the league games resume.

A defeat in the tenth round of EPL matches for any of the Premier League managers most at risk was sure to put them in immediate danger.

With Pierre Sage and Crystal Palace the only ones towards the bottom to lose that weekend, it seemingly sealed that Palace manager’s fate.

#1986. West Ham Winger Faces Another Fitness Test As Parker Waits

West Ham United are facing something of a dilemma over Manor Solomon, with Israel reportedly considering bringing the winger back into the team for Tuesday’s Nations League clash against Austria. The 26-year-old has been struggling with back pain during the international break, although Israel manager Ran Ben-Shimon has suggested that he is feeling better after returning to training.

According to Sport5, Solomon could now be in contention for the Austria fixture. That follows comments from Ben-Shimon suggesting the player had trained and was feeling better, although his fitness would need to be reassessed.

For West Ham manager Scott Parker, however, the situation presents an interesting dilemma. We desperately need the old Manor Solomon back, but I wonder whether another international appearance is really what the player needs right now.

Manor Solomon representing Israel during a difficult international break. The West Ham winger has been carrying a back injury since October

Look, I’m caught between a rock and a hard place on this one.

There is part of me that hopes Solomon gets a game, so he can get back to form. Because there’s no doubt about it, West Ham have a far bigger chance of getting promoted this season if Manor Solomon is back to the sort of form he was in when he played for Leeds in the Championship.

Clearly Scott Parker has faith in him because he has seen how destructive he can be in that division. Getting that player back would be a significant boost for the Hammers, particularly with the Championship promotion race starting to get serious.

But, and it’s a big but, we have had complaints of back injury during the October internationals, and we’ve already had it during this international break.

As I reported earlier in October, a West Ham source confirmed that Solomon was in considerable pain after an exhausting international schedule. More recently, we reported on his latest back problem, which restricted his training with Israel.

There is also part of me that wonders whether we would not have been better served, and the player himself, actually resting up, getting some medical treatment, or even being given ten days off completely to recuperate and joining back up with the squad for the last few days of training before the Preston game.

As things stand, there’s nothing in his recent form that suggests he could start and should start against Preston. And without him being on the training pitch during this international break to impress Scott Parker, he’s not going to be able to catch the manager’s eye.

Edvin Austbø has certainly given Parker something to think about on the left wing. Indeed, Austbø’s recent performances have highlighted the competition for Solomon’s place, and I suspect the Norwegian is currently ahead of him in the pecking order.

But I don’t want to write off Solomon. We know what he’s capable of producing in this division, and West Ham will need every bit of attacking quality available if we’re serious about getting back into the Premier League.

Hopefully, Israel will make the sensible decision and only involve him against Austria if he is genuinely fit enough to play. We cannot afford another international break to leave us with a player who returns to east London carrying another injury.

#1985. ‘I felt my leg…’ – Dominik Szoboszlai makes worrying injury admission after Hungary win

Dominik Szoboszlai has given an update on his knee injury after Hungary’s win over Georgia on Saturday, and his comments could be quite concerning for Liverpool fans.

The midfielder’s involvement for his country during this international window was placed in doubt after the knock that he incurred in the Reds’ victory at Crystal Palace last weekend, although he still linked up with Marco Rossi’s squad for their UEFA Nations League fixtures.

The Hungarian FA had deferred any decision on whether the 26-year-old would play until the last minute, but he featured for the entirety of his nation’s 2-0 triumph in Tbilisi and claimed the assist for Barnabas Varga’s clinching goal.

Szoboszlai revealed after the match that he nearly pulled out of playing after he felt a twinge during the warm-up prior to kick-off, but his determination to feature would eventually prevail.

In quotes relayed by Nemzeti Sport, the Hungary captain said: “I was always 100% sure that I would be able to play, but the doctors were less sure. I progressed day by day, focused on myself, received treatment.

“I played with my leg for a training session and a half, and in the warm-up I was close to cancelling it because I felt my leg on one of the shots, but if I’ve come this far, I won’t let the team down. Now the treatment starts all over again. I have to be ready again by Tuesday.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Szoboszlai’s comments may well come as a worry to Liverpool fans, with the midfielder admitting that he played through the pain barrier and seemingly defied the assessment of medical professionals.

His remark about getting ready for Hungary’s match against Northern Ireland on Tuesday night will also have Andoni Iraola sweating, with the 26-year-old set to push himself for a tight turnaround even though he seems nowhere near full fitness.

It’s natural that, as captain of his country, the Reds’ number 8 will stop at nothing to try and be available for them, but his club will be left praying that he comes through the Magyars’ next game unscathed.

Szoboszlai will return from international duty into a hectic run of 11 Liverpool fixtures before the end of December, and we’ll need him and his teammates to be operating at their best throughout that busy period.

For everyone at Anfield, Hungary’s match on Tuesday will be monitored with frayed nerves to see if the midfielder comes through without any further complications in his knee.

#1983. International quality Newcastle United defence that will provide platform for success

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The Newcastle United defence has been the subject of much focus this season.

Not a lot of the debate on it has been positive.

So has the criticism that’s come the way of the Newcastle United defence been fair?

In the ten Premier League matches so far, this has been the story of the Newcastle United defence.

Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 2 Liverpool 2 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Spurs 0 Newcastle 2 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 2 Bournemouth 2 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Leeds 4 Newcastle 1 Lewis Miley, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 2 Hull 1 Lewis Miley, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Coventry 4 Newcastle 1 Lewis Miley, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 0 Aston Villa 1 Amar Dedić, Fabian Schar, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall – Crystal Palace 0 Newcastle 2 Amar Dedić, Fabian Schar, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 0 Everton 1 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall – Fulham 1 Newcastle 1

What I think should be acknowledged first of all, is that we have lacked a settled Newcastle United defence. Injuries playing havoc.

Secondly, there has been undeniable improvement. The Newcastle United defence leaked 13 goals in the opening six Premier League matches, only three goals conceded in the last four. In the last six and half hours (including added time) of Premier League action, United conceding just those three goals, an average of around a goal conceded each 130 minutes following the defeat at Coventry.

This is not to say the United defence were almost faultless, more a case of they are improving.

When you look at those three goals that were conceded most recently in the Premier League, it gives added information. The Villa goal came when a cross from the right eluded Lewis Miley, a midfielder playing out of position at right-back. The Everton one was pure and simply a poor error from Lukas Hornicek who allowed a low standard cross to squirm under. Then the one at Fulham came via deflections off both Thiaw (in the build up) and Burn (to turn it beyond Hornicek.

Yes the opposition had other chances in these games but not loads.

Reality is as well that if Newcastle United had managed at the other end to score a couple of goals in each of these last four matches then it would have been 12 points out of 12 in the last quartet of Premier League games.

That is very different to the opening half dozen EPL matches, where Newcastle United scored six goals in the four games against Liverpool, Coventry, Leeds and Bournemouth but that only brought two points from a possible 12. The Newcastle United defending a lot better against Tottenham and Hull for the two victories early on, with only a single goal conceded in more than three hours of football against that pair.

Now though I think things could go to another level again with this Newcastle United defence, if a bit of fair luck starts going our way on the injury and fitness front.

An international level Newcastle United defence.

Lewis Hall is brilliant, for England and Newcastle United. Surely no doubters amongst you on that one.

Dan Burn has been a huge miss in the opening seven Premier League matches this season. No coincidence only two goals conceded in the three EPL matches he has started on his return after a length injury spell. He has now backed that up with how he has performed for England in recent days.

We saw last season how good Malick Thiaw can be and I think the Fulham match definitely suggested than alongside Dan Burn we could at last have the best available partnership in place finally, of the current NUFC squad. Thiaw has started the last three Germany matches under Jurgen Klopp and they have only conceded one goal.

Tino Livramento was back in the Premier League matchday squad at Fulham and these couple of weeks should have brought him along further. For me there is no doubt about Tino’s quality, the problem has been getting him injury free and back to full fitness on a consistent basis.

Lukas Hornicek has had an up and down start with Newcastle United but taking everything into consideration, I think he has shown plenty to suggest he can do well, especially if he has a regular back four in front of him who have the capacity to give him decent protection week in week out.

Having the three England internationals and our German international making up a Newcastle United back four has huge potential to build the kind of solid platform NUFC need this season.

If Tino Livramento continues to have injury and fitness issues, I believe Amar Dedić is capable of doing a very good job in his absence. I think the Bosnian defender has done okay overall so far, having made the huge step up to the Premier League and walking into what was a chaotic NUFC situation.

If we can have the Newcastle United defence performing consistently well, that then gives us far more chance of improving things further up the pitch, helping United to have far more control of matches and giving a much more positive platform for midfielders and attacking players to prosper.

The player was said to be hugely keen on the move but his club refused to sanction the deal that would have brought the 20-goal Bundesliga 2 talent to West Ham.

The Hammers settled on Joel Piroe instead, but were apparently hankering after another crack at signing Ali Zoma in January.

Their article: “Miroslav Klose hands West Ham transfer blow” describes the shoulder injury sustained by the striker which more or less rules him out of West Ham’s thinking for the winter window.

Coming hot on the heels of yesterday’s report claiming Rangers’ Ryan Naderi wasn’t interested on a move to London Stadium it is clear that Koppen has his work cut out to bring a new front man to Scott Parker’s squad. Sliding towards mid table in the Championship will not make his task any easier so there will be added incentive for the Irons to start looking like genuine title contenders once again in what remains of this year in order to attract the best crop of talent in the transfer window ahead.

There must be a sense of disappointment amongst West Ham’s academy that one of their much-heralded strikers, poached from north of the border in July 2025, hasn’t yet progressed on a more impressive trajectory.

After all, Daniel Cummings joined West Ham as the latest nineteen year old striker ‘wonderkid’ with Champions League experience having featured in Celtic’s European campaign before quitting the club and heading for east London last summer.

Sending the young forward out on loan to fifth-tier Aldershot Town (no disrespect to Aldershot) could be seen as West Ham’s tacit admission that the striker has not yet delivered on the precocious talent he displayed in Celtic’s youth team scoring, seemingly, at will.

Fellow academy Scot Josh Landers is at Ayr United on loan

Of course, there’s a certain amount of schadenfreude from his old club. Celtic fan site celticshorts.com proclaim with glee the apparent stalling of Cummings’ progress:

Which Cummings will just have to deal with, get his head down, score some goals and answer the criticism from his former club in the best possible way.

#1980. ‘Looking back…’ – Alexander Isak speaks out over penalty controversy in defeat to Arsenal

Alexander Isak has spoken out about the controversial penalty incident in which he was involved during Liverpool’s defeat to Arsenal a fortnight ago.

Five minutes after Kai Havertz netted the only goal of the match, the Reds’ number 9 had his shirt pulled by Jurrien Timber inside the box, but neither on-field referee Andy Madley nor Stuart Attwell on VAR deemed it to have been a foul.

The transgression was unmistakably clear on replays, and the Premier League’s Key Match Incidents panel has since acknowledged that a spot kick should’ve been awarded.

Speaking to reporters whilst on international duty with Sweden, Isak was asked if he felt that he should’ve had a penalty.

He replied (Aftonbladet, via Liverpool Echo): “Yeah, looking back I suppose it does look that way, but when you’re in the moment, you don’t always perceive exactly what’s happening.

“I could feel myself being pulled a bit, but not to the extent that it appears later on. I was focused on scoring. It’s hard to try to score and then fall down at the same time. I was so locked in on the goal that I didn’t really register it.”

On whether he should’ve gone to ground to try and sway the referee, Isak said: “I don’t think there’s any need to embellish or go down on purpose. Sure, if I’d had a better read on the situation, I might have made sure the referee noticed it, that’s about all you can do, but I don’t believe you need to dive or exaggerate in situations like this.

“Perhaps it shouldn’t even matter that much, given that we have VAR and systems in place to make the decisive calls in these kinds of moments.”

Isak is absolutely right in saying that a penalty should’ve been awarded, and that he shouldn’t have to act unnaturally to convince the referee to give the decision in his team’s favour.

Andoni Iraola remarked after the game that a spot kick probably would’ve been given if the Liverpool striker had gone to ground, but the onus isn’t on players to sway the officials – it’s on the latter to get these big calls right, especially with recourse to VAR.

It feels as though the debate about officiating in the Premier League will continue indefinitely, with no discernible sign of an improvement in standards from Pro Ref figurehead Howard Webb.

It’s to Isak’s great credit that he’s given such a calm and measured verdict on the penalty incident when he and his team were so blatantly wronged. He’d have had every right to complain profusely about what happened; we’d suspect that many other players would’ve done so if they were in that situation.

He certainly hasn’t let it bother him in terms of his contributions on the pitch, with the 27-year-old scoring in Liverpool’s subsequent games against Fenerbahce and Crystal Palace to take his tally for the season to eight goals in 14 matches across all competitions.

That is, in fact, the best response to the injustice which was done against him Anfield two weeks ago.

#1978. West Ham Fans Asked to Unite in Memory of 19-Year-Old Supporter Luke

The loss of a young person reverberates far beyond their immediate family. Today, we are sharing Luke’s story in the hope of raising awareness, encouraging compassion, and supporting a tribute that means so much to those left behind.

Remembering Luke: A Young Life Gone Too Soon

At just 19 years old, Luke’s life was tragically cut short, leaving a family, circle of friends, and wider community struggling to come to terms with an unimaginable loss.

Known affectionately as “Lukey” and “Little Man” by those closest to him, Luke was a devoted West Ham United supporter and a loyal season ticket holder.

As they continue to navigate their grief, Luke’s family have made a simple but heartfelt request.

They are asking West Ham supporters attending the upcoming home fixture against Preston to join together in a minute of applause during the 19th minute of the match, marking the age at which Luke passed away.

The tribute is intended as a celebration of his life and a visible reminder that no family should feel alone during their darkest moments.

A shirt bearing Luke’s name will be placed on his seat in the stadium, providing a poignant symbol of the empty space left by his passing.

By sharing Luke’s story, we hope not only to support his family but also to encourage conversations around loss, grief, and the importance of supporting one another through difficult times.

C&H encourage anyone attending the match, or anyone who sees Luke’s story online, to help spread the word and support the planned tribute.

On the 19th minute, every clap will be a reminder that Luke’s life touched many people and that his memory continues to live on through his family, friends, and fellow supporters.

Our thoughts are with everyone who knew and loved Luke.

If this story resonates with you, please share it to help ensure Luke receives the tribute his family and friends are hoping for. Sometimes the smallest act of support can make the biggest difference.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

#1977. West Ham player’s incredible injury statistic shows why he was the bargain of the summer

How managers and fitness conditioning teams must dread these international breaks – a player coming back with a serious injury picked up on duty for the national side must be every coaches’ fear. it seems a case of ‘so far so good’ for West Ham’s “international brigade” with no reports filtering through to Hammers HQ of new issues.

That does however leave the pre-existing condition: Manor Solomon’s frank admission to his national press will hardly reassure anyone at Rush Green. The winger has been struggling with a back injury and, according to sportwitness, this is neither a new issue nor one aggravated through too many games in the last window – which saw players asked to compete four times in twelve days for their nations:

“My back is something I’ve been dealing with for many years, ever since I was a teenager. I felt it during Saturday’s game; when I joined the national team, I felt fine, but by Tuesday, it had got worse, and I couldn’t train,” he said.

“Everyone knows how important the national team is to me and how hard it is for me to watch the team play while I’m not on the field. I hope I’ll be able to play on Tuesday.”

Facing a late fitness test, it seems Solomon is putting caution to one side in his desperation to be part of the Israel national team to take on Austria tomorrow.

Sadly, there is nothing new here, the old ‘club v country‘ debate in which domestic football (paying the players’ massive wages) gets a lesser priority from a player who will stop at nothing and go through the pain to play for his country.

Solomon looked like the deal of the decade after his first couple of outings, having joined West Ham for a mere £5 million up front.

More disclosures about his back issues and many and varied other problems – which have led him to sit out an incredible 860 days since the start of his career in 2018 ( according to sportwitness) make the price look more understandable by the week.

West Ham will have to cope with a player who has huge fitness issues but who doesn’t apparently, want to listen to his body, rather playing through the pain to represent his country. It’s not a combination that is likely preserve his longevity in the sport.
