#1908. ‘With the times’ Scotland boss won me over with surprise call - here’s why he’s different to Steve Clarke

Scotland striker Che Adams admits he was instantly won over by head coach Sebastien Pocognoli after a surprise FaceTime call from the Belgian when he was out injured last month.

Adams, 30, was ruled out of Pocognoli’s inaugural camp in October after picking up a thigh injury with club side Torino, but was restored to the Scotland starting XI for their 2-1 win over North Macedonia on Friday night, and registered an assist for the first of John McGinn’s two goals.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

After being regular for former manager Steve Clarke during his seven year reign, Adams admits Scotland’s early performances under their new 38-year-old manager have been patchy so far. Still ironing out the teething issues often faced by teams in transition, he concedes they are yet to click, but says the squad believe in Pocognoli and his new methods.

Get our daily football newsletter by clicking here.

“The camps haven’t changed much but the manager is definitely more intense,” said Adams. “I think it’s the European style of play and thinking. It’s going to take time for him to understand the boys, understand us as players and understand us as a squad. This gaffer has good ideas, a good approach to the game. Everyone’s buying into it and I definitely think we’ll see the benefits.

“With Steve [Clarke] you could have a laugh and you can do that with this gaffer as well, but he’s a lot more intense in terms of detail, off the pitch telling you where to be and what to do. In the last camp when I was out injured he was on asking how my injury was, how long I’d be out for and if I still wanted to be part of it.

“Coming off a transitional period like we have just now, it’s difficult to know where you are and what you want to do. But all the boys here want to play for our country and do Scotland proud. I had no doubts about it, it’s good to get away from Italy for a while, be around some good lads.”

Striking trio Kieron Bowie, Oli McBurnie and Robbie Ure were all called into the squad by Pocognoli for last month’s Nations League games against Slovenia, North Macedonia and Switzerland, with Adams injured and Lyndon Dykes and George Hirst both left out.

With enhanced competition for a starting spot, the Torino hitman said the Belgian ensured he kept in contact with him during his injury layoff, revealing the unique method Pocognoli implemented with the team since he was appointed manager in August.

“I heard from the manager the last time when I wasn’t in the camp,” said Adams. “He loves a FaceTime call. I think he’s taken a few of the boys by surprise when they’ve been out walking their dogs and stuff. I think KT [Kieran Tierney] was out for a walk when he phoned him. He just calls out of the blue and has done it to a few of the boys. It’s unexpected and it’s different because we’ve never experienced something like that, but it’s good.

“The manager is with the times, really, he’s brought in his new ideas. He’s a few years younger and has a different philosophy on how he wants his team to play. It just takes time to click but it’s up to us as players now to show we can do what he wants. We have been together for a number of years now so we know each other’s game. You could see on Friday us starting to put the manager’s things in practice, we won a lot of balls high with our pressing.

“For me, it’s a bit different to what I’m used to at club level because that’s a little bit more free. I can roam where I want in and around the back line for my club, but I am enjoying it. When you’re playing with boys like John McGinn and Scott McTominay who have the creativity, that eye for goal and pass forward that you don’t really get at club level it is good.

“The gaffer wanted me to run deep on Friday as well, so nothing changed there. As games go on, stretching the opposition helps John and Scott get on the ball where they can hurt teams with their creativity. You can definitely see things are coming together, you could see how we were building up and playing out. You have to credit the manager for putting the belief in the young players who have come in as well.”

#1905. Scotland face a mountainous task - but rewards are worth the climb

To emphasis the scale of what faces Scotland at the Sitterstadion in St Gallen on Monday night, the national team is looking to repeat a feat only carried out by Germany and Spain over the past two years.

Switzerland don’t lose often on home soil under Murat Yakin. The Germans and the world champions have prevailed in the Alps that period. In short, it takes a very good performance to leave with the full loot. And for Scotland to stand a chance in achieving their objective and finishing second in Nations League Group B1, they need to win.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Even then, it might not be enough. Sitting third on seven points going into Monday’s final round of matches, Scotland trail second-placed Slovenia by a point. Should the Slovenians defeat bottom-of-the-table North Macedonia in Skopje, the Scots could win 5-0 and it wouldn’t change the standings.

A draw won’t help either, as Slovenia have a better head-to-head record over Scotland by virtue of their 2-1 win at Hampden last month.

Ending up second is important. It would move Scotland into a play-off spot and a chance of promotion to Nations League A. It would also ensure a second seeding for the Euro 2028 qualification draw next month. Scotland are a host nation for the tournament, and getting in through the back door of a reserved place for non-qualifiers would be embarrassing - although not as humiliating as not being there at all.

The odds of toppling Slovenia, however, are stacked against Scotland. It requires two surprise results. North Macedonia have been meek throughout this campaign and have no points to show for their name, even if their display at Hampden on Friday showed glimmers of improvement in a 2-1 loss. The Scots need a favour in the Balkans.

Switzerland may give Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli some optimism. Yakin is planning to shuffle his pack after landing top spot with a game to spare. Some of the star Swiss names may be kept in reserve. Granit Xhaka, Manuel Akanji, Dan Ndoye and Johan Manzambi are definitely out.

Nevertheless, Yakin vowed that his team will still be strong,. “It has happened a few times already. But we will make sure we get good level of player onto the pitch.

“It’s good thing we have won the group already. It’s now an opportunity to make changes. It doesn’t make sense to wait for injuries players. We have enough opportunities and possibilities.

“We will rotate a but but we first have to make sure that we have a stable defence with experienced defenders. Of course, we will try to get as many players involved as possible. There are a lot of players who haven’t played at all, so they can play from the start.

“We want our boys to get a chance and look forward to it and show their best game. We will certainly make some changes in attack.”

It is of benefit to Scotland that they face an opponent with nothing on the line. Especially as there are areas of concern over how the team has fared so far under Pocognoli’s watch.

The game against Switzerland will be Pocognoli’s sixth in charge after two wins against North Macedonia, two defeats (Switzerland and Slovenia at home) and a draw in Ljubljana. The performance on Friday was far from convincing, but for Pocognoli to get his first win at Hampden should have lifted a bit of weight from the 39-year-old Belgian’s shoulders.

Pocognoli stuck with a back three and Ryan Porteous, Luke Graham and Kieran Tierney coped pretty well with North Macedonia’s blunt attack. The visitors’ goal came from a set-piece and they didn’t look good enough to score in open play, even if they had attacking moments.

The worry for many Scotland fans is that better teams will punish Scotland when they either counter-attack or break through the press. Pocognoli’s insistence on playing a high line and asking his team to be proactive most of the time means that the defence does get exposed. And the top teams will take advantage.

Shorn of many defenders, it is likely Pocognoli will stick with the same back three. There is clamour for a back four, but the head coach will surely be reluctant to throw away all of his work thus far. His biggest conundrum is whether to keep winger Ben Gannon-Doak as his right wing-back or deploy the more rounded and defensively-savvy Aaron Hickey there.

On the other flank, a massive piece of history will be made. Captain Andy Robertson will win his 103rd cap and become Scotland’s most-capped male player of all time. It is an incredible achievement for the 32-year-old, who has been front and centre of Scotland’s recent renaissance and while he will try to shrug off the limelight, this night does belong to him.

Robertson will not want such a milestone tarnished by a defeat and neither will his team-mates. “It just takes time to click but it’s up to us as players now to show we can do what he wants,” said striker Che Adams of Pocognoli’s philosophy. “We have been together for a number of years now so we know each other’s game. You could see on Friday us starting to put the manager’s things in practice, we won a lot of balls high with our pressing.

“Coming off a transitional period like we have just now, it’s difficult to know where you are and what you want to do. But all the boys here want to play for our country and do Scotland proud.”

A win in Switzerland would do the nation proud. Depending on what happens 990 miles down the road in Skopje, it may or may not be enough to finish second in the group, but a positive display would give Scotland something to build upon next year when the Euro 2028 qualifiers start and give a sceptical public reasons for optimism.

Following their narrow defeat to high-flying Roffey the previous weekend, Common once again demonstrated their resilience and fighting spirit, giving as good as they got against a strong United side.

The visitors defended heroically for long periods of the opening half whilst also posing a threat at the other end, creating several opportunities of their own.

Goalkeeper Matt Cruttwell continued his impressive recent form, producing two smart early saves to deny the hosts and keep the scores level. At the other end, Ollie Hull came close to breaking the deadlock following a superb mazy run, weaving his way through the home defence before firing narrowly wide of the target.

Sam Ellis then went even closer to giving Common the lead when he cut inside from the left and unleashed a goal-bound effort, only to be denied by an excellent save from the United goalkeeper.

Despite Common's encouraging display, it was the hosts who struck first in the 36th minute. Jorge Nones found himself in space on the edge of the penalty area and slid the ball home to give United a slender advantage heading into the interval.

There was then a moment of controversy when Freddie Warren appeared to be brought down whilst racing through on goal, but despite Common's appeals, the referee waved play on.

With the visitors continuing to battle for an equaliser, Cruttwell was once again called into action, producing another excellent save to deny James Stone and keep Common firmly in the contest.

As the game entered its closing stages, Common continued to push forward in search of an equaliser, but their hopes of taking something from the afternoon were finally extinguished two minutes from time.

Substitute James Hull raced through on goal and calmly slotted the ball past Cruttwell to double United's advantage and secure all three points for the hosts.

Common boss Russ Eldridge said: “I thought the lads were excellent again on Saturday. We've now played two of the best sides in the division in successive weeks and competed really well against both.

“We knew Eastbourne would have plenty of the ball, but we defended brilliantly at times and created some very good opportunities ourselves. On another day, we could easily have gone in front, and I think that would have changed the game.

“I was disappointed with the decision when Freddie went through in the second half. From where I was standing, it looked a clear foul, and those are the decisions you need to go your way in tight games like this.

“Matt has been outstanding for us recently, but I thought everyone put in a tremendous shift. The second goal came when we were pushing to get something from the game, which was frustrating.

“The performances are certainly improving, and the lads deserve enormous credit for their attitude and commitment. However, we can't keep talking about playing well and coming away with nothing. We need to start turning these performances into points, and hopefully that will happen sooner rather than later.”

#1902. I watched Scotland sneak past Wallabies and noted two big replacement plus Rangers stars in stands

Scotland got back on the winning trail with a 15-12 victory over Australia at Murrayfield.

After the disappointment of losing heavily to New Zealand eight days ago, head coach Gregor Townsend will have been pleased to see his team recover - although the triumph was far from swashbuckling.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Mark Atkinson was at Murrayfield to cover proceedings for The Scotsman and picks out some talking points from the match:

Winning was clearly the most important thing for Scotland, which is why with eight minutes to go, Finn Russell took the three points from a penalty rather than going for touch to push for a try.

It moved Scotland ten points clear and left Australia with too much to do, even with Max Jorgensen’s late try to keep the game very close.

However, Scotland’s inability to rack up the points is likely to harm them in the wider scale of the Nations Championship.

With one round of fixtures remaining before finals weekend, Scotland sit fourth in the standings on 15 points with a points difference of -8. After their historic win over New Zealand, fifth-placed Wales also have 15 points but with a points difference of -28. They face Australia next, which is winnable.

Scotland take on whipping boys Japan at Murrayfield on Saturday and need to win comprehensively with a bonus point to put pressure on third-placed Ireland and second-placed England, who are on 20 points and have points differences of +57 and +134 respectively.

Ireland take on South Africa and England face New Zealand, where a solitary bonus point will ensure either of them a top-three finish - and given England’s point difference, it would take something special to overhaul them. Scotland's best hope is probably a big Springbok win.

The chances are Scotland will finish fourth - which would mean a play-off against either Argentina or Australia.

Scotland did not play with much verve or pizzazz and were lamentably wasteful at the start of the second half when Billy Pollard was sent to the sin bin. Rather than adding to the scoreboard, they gave away two cheap penalties and lost their own lineout in a promising position.

Playmaker Russell failed to ignite the game and was patchy with some of his kicking, while the ball very rarely made it out to the wide players.

It wasn’t a game that got the pulses racing and Scotland will likely pay the price.

While both teams will rue not scoring a bucketload of points, there will be some satisfaction from the defensive effort given what happened the previous weekend.

Scotland shipped 43 points to the All Blacks and Australia were on the end of 45 points at Twickenham. It was evident that both sides were intent on keeping the door shut.

While imagination was at a premium, there were a lot of good tackles and discipline when pressure was on. Australia boss Les Kiss referenced it afterwards and Townsend will be pleased with the way his team held firm in difficult conditions for the majority of the final 20 minutes.

Darcy Graham’s tackle right at the end on Tom Wright ensured the win for Scotland and must be applauded for his work at the death.

Scotland had to turn to their bench before and after kick-off, and the replacements did themselves no harm.

Tom Jordan was a last-minute sub for captain Sione Tuipulotu, who failed a late fitness test due to a knee injury. The Bristol Bears man is a versatile fellow and while he’s more often than not been used at 10 or 15 for Scotland, he was asked to partner Huw Jones at centre.

This wasn’t a game for creativity, but Jordan did have some nice offloads and he defended well. If Tuipulotu doesn’t make next week against Japan, Jordan has probably kept himself ahead of Stafford McDowall.

In the pack, Scott Cummings pulled up on 25 minutes and the lock was replaced by his Glasgow Warriors club-mate Max Williamson, who made his presence felt with some big hits and powerful work at the breakdown.

Williamson has found himself behind Cummings and another Glasgow man in Gregor Brown, but this was a performance that will give Townsend food for thought for the rest of the year.

Blair Kinghorn used to be a nailed-on starter for Scotland, but his own form at Toulouse, niggling injuries and the emergence of Kyle Rowe at Glasgow Warriors has put his position in jeopardy.

Townsend gave Kinghorn the whole match at full-back and he served up a reminder of why he can make a difference in the Test arena.

He was secure under the high ball, ran with purpose and broke the line on several occasions. He also put in an excellent tackle on Jorgensen at a crucial point in the game.

Many feel Rowe was unfortunate not to feature against Australia, but Kinghorn has that little bit extra physicality and oomph that sets him apart.

We are also in the midst of an international break in football and that allowed a couple of Rangers players to take in this match.

Scotland striker Lawrence Shankland and Australia midfielder Cammy Devlin are both currently injured, so they were able to watch on in the Murrayfield stands without any commitments - and not far from their old stomping ground.

The ex-Hearts duo seemed to be enjoying the game and Shankland will no doubt have liked Scotland landing the bragging rights over the Wallabies.

#1901. The little-known new face called up by England: Can you name the star brought in to replace Ezri Konsa?

Published: 05:58 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 12:26 EST, 10 November 2026

Thomas Tuchel has made a first-time England call-up to replace Ezri Konsa - but casual fans could be forgiven if they do not recognise the latest Three Lions addition.

He is not a widely-recognised face among the stars from the Premier League and other top European leagues in Tuchel's selection but James Hill, 24, has starred for Bournemouth in their eight-match winning run under Marco Rose this season.

The central defender, who started his career at Fleetwood Town, has enjoyed a dream few months: He married partner Tara Rose in June, welcomed his first child in August and has now had his maiden England call.

England announced today that Arsenal defender Konsa will not be in contention to face Croatia at Wembley on Thursday night - although he will be fit to potentially face Spain away on Sunday - and Hill has been called up in his place.

Hill has played for England's Under 20s and Under 21s but this is his first senior call. He was signed by Bournemouth for just £1.2million in 2022 - beating Sheffield United, Burnley, Leeds, Southampton, Tottenham and even Barcelona, who all checked on his progress.

Bournemouth's official X account posted today: 'Congratulations, Hilly. Our defender has earned a first senior @England call-up.'

James Hill - pictured with new wife Tara - has been called up to the latest England squad (Source: Instagram/james_hill_10)

Hill has starred for Bournemouth in their eight-match winning run under Marco Rose

Hill's route to the top is a fascinating one. He attended a trial day at Fleetwood as a 14-year-old and managed to impress them enough to earn place at their new academy.

Interestingly, Hill did not play for a football team of any kind before he was 10, simply kicking a ball around with friends and playing in the garden to hone his skills.

Blackpool opted against signing him after a trial and he was then dropped by Bolton after a short stint.

It proved to be a shrewd piece of talent identification from Fleetwood, with Hill later becoming the club's record sale, eclipsing the fee they received for Jamie Vardy.

And having signed for the Cherries in 2022, Hill has now established himself as a key member of Marco Rose's side.

He's played every minute of every Premier League match this season at the heart of the defence and clearly Tuchel has been impressed.

Speaking before his call-up, Hill said: 'It’s every kid’s dream, isn’t it? You grow up watching the Three Lions on TV, for the World Cup, the Euros. It’s one of the greatest honours you can have in football.'

Football is in the blood for Hill. His father, Matt, made more than 550 appearances in the Football League for the likes of Preston North End, Wolverhampton Wanderers, Sheffield United and Queens Park Rangers as a defender.

Hill played for England at age group level, pictured here kissing his now wife after a game

Hill's younger brother, Tyler, is also in the game, playing for Torquay United in National League South.

But Matt did not pressure his sons into the sport, with James previously telling the Times: 'He didn’t want me to feel as though it’s a job.

'He wanted me to feel like I’m wanting to be here because I love doing it. This is my passion. It brings me happiness. He wanted me to come to that conclusion, not for him to make that decision for me.'

Hill was a well-rounded sportsman and his secondary school did not even play football. Instead, he excelled as a fly-half for the rugby side and impressed as a javelin thrower.

He attributes his success as being aided by trying his hand at different disciplines and it is paying off in abundance having had to largely bide his time before earning a first-team spot under Andoni Iraola last term, with loans to Blackburn and Hearts helping him develop.

Hill's progress flew somewhat under the radar somewhat for many fans outside of Bournemouth and his career peak of an England call-up coincides with domestic bliss.

Having married Tara in the summer, they welcomed their daughter Edie two months later.

Hill, pictured, heading the ball away against Ipswich has become one of the best defenders in the Premier League

'Becoming a dad is one of the most special things I’ve ever experienced in my life,' he said. 'There isn’t a manual though, it’s just like, "Congratulations, you’ve got a baby". Then the door shuts! Hang on a minute. What am I supposed to do next? Is there a book for this? My wife has been absolutely incredible.'

He regularly shares pictures from both his professional and personal life on social media, putting wedding snaps alongside action shots of Bournemouth games.

Hill's England call-up will no doubt introduce him to a whole new audience previously unaware of the defender's capabilities, with only 34,000 Instagram followers at present.

The 24-year-old must now impress Tuchel enough to earn some game time when England play Croatia on Thursday in their next Nations League encounter.

#1899. Celtic treble winner promises to ‘lead change in football’ as he launches bid to overthrow Infantino

Former Celtic defender Ramon Vega has confirmed that he is launching a bid to replace Gianni Infantino as FIFA President at next year’s elections, saying that football must be “for the people, not those who control it.”

Vega, 55, spent a brief but memorable loan spell at Celtic in the second half of the 2000/01 campaign, scoring twice on his debut in a 6-0 win over Aberdeen. He also had spells at Tottenham Hotspur and Cagliari during his 13-year career, and earned 23 caps for Switzerland.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

During his six-month loan stint at Celtic Park, Vega quickly developed into a fan favourite as part of a Martin O'Neill side that lifted a domestic treble in 2001. However, his stay in Glasgow was brief, and he signed for Watford on a free transfer shortly afterwards, after the London club offered him the security of a longer contract at Vicarage Road.

Retiring two years later, he has forged a successful career in global finance and asset management, but Vega now believes the time is right to oust under-pressure President Infantino when the elections formally take place at the 77th FIFA Congress in Rabat, Morocco next March.

The Swiss defender, who can speak six languages, has ran for the role three times previously, in 2015, 2019 and 2023, but maintains his belief that he can succeed in his bid to become the next FIFA President, stating that “football stands at a defining crossroads” and that “the decisions we make today will shape the future of our beautiful game for generations to come.”

Writing on his official X (formerly Twitter) account, he said on Sunday: “A credible FIFA begins with a credible election. UEFA provided Infantino with €500,000 in official campaign funding to support his global travel and logistics ahead of the February 2016 FIFA Extraordinary Congress. Europe played a decisive role in bringing the current leadership to FIFA therefore also has a huge responsibility to help bring about change.

“I call for open and transparent dialogue across the entire global football family. Major decisions affecting our game should never be imposed. They must follow genuine consultation, where every voice is heard and the broadest possible consensus is built before decisions are made. The solution is a credible candidate, a democratic election, a clear program capable of restoring trust, integrity, transparency and unity.

“I offer every member association a neutral, independent and credible democratic alternative, a candidate rooted in the game, who can bridge football and international finance &business, bring cultures together and lead FIFA with competence, integrity and independence. For me serving football is not about personal ambition. It's a responsibility, a duty and a matter of honour.”

To officially run for the Presidency, the former Celtic man must win the backing of five or more national federations before Wednesday’s [November 18] deadline. However, this could be possible, with Vega claiming he has backing across every continent, though he has yet to reveal who is endorsing him.

#1896. Rangers star saved by Man Utd man as team secure quarter-final place with stunning comeback

Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin breathed a sigh of relief after seeing the penalty he conceded just minutes after his introduction to the pitch saved by Manchester United goalkeeper Senne Lammens during Belgium’s thumping 4-1 win over Italy in the Nations League on Sunday night.

Despite starting Belgium’s 2-1 win away over Turkiye on Thursday night, the Rangers star had to be content with a place on the bench against Italy as Mark van Bommel’s side looked to seal a place in the quarter-finals of the Nations League at the Stade Roi Baudouin.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Two points ahead of their visitors ahead of the Group A1 clash on nine points, the game got off to a disastrous start for the hosts when Italy went into an 11th-minute lead when Brentford defender Michael Kayode's cross to Pio Esposito to score 10th international goal in 15 appearances.

However, the lead was short-lived, and Belgium found themselves back on level terms just four minutes later when Brighton wing-back Maxim de Cuyper slammed home to restore parity in Brussels, before centre-back Nathan Ngoy rifled home from close range after a scramble in the box on 22 minutes.

Jeremy Doku then completed the turnaround when he added a third for Belgium just four minutes later, dancing through the Italian defence with stunning footwork before firing a low drive beyond his Manchester City teammate Gianluigi Donnarumma in the visitor’s goal. The strike put his side temporarily top of Group A1, with Turkiye holding France to a 0-0 draw at half-time.

With 10 minutes to spare, Diego Moreira made sure of the win when he neatly placed home his side’s fourth of the game after being teed up by Kevin De Bruyne. However, it was not enough to seal top spot in the group, with Belgium forced to be content with qualification to the Nations League quarter-finals via second place as France ran out 2-1 winners in Paris.

Despite the Group standings being all but confirmed, the action did not cease, with Italy awarded a last-minute penalty after VAR ruled that Raskin had handled Alphadjo Cisse’s shot in the area. The Rangers man had replaced Romeo Lavia just over 10 minutes earlier, but needn’t have worried, as goalkeeper Lammens pulled off an excellent save to deny Esposito a brace.

“If Donnarumma had not been in goal, then we would've scored six,” said new Belgium head coach van Bommel. “I'll be honest, I didn't expect this when we started two months ago, but even before that first match with Italy, I could tell this was a really intelligent group of players. That makes it a pleasure for a coach to work with them.

“These players can anticipate an opponent, are flexible, and can adapt to different situations. Today you saw that reflected. Not only was the idea right, individually many players stepped up too. And ultimately we managed to dominate an opponent like Italy for long periods. That is the most important thing to me."

Belgium will discover their Nations League quarter-final opponents on Friday, November 20, 2026, with the draw set to take place at 11am UK time in Nyon, Switzerland.

#1895. Outstanding Leeds cut short Jaissle’s Newcastle honeymoon

The noise started in a corner of the South Stand, early in the second half. It was muffled at first, but as the ball popped from one white shirt to another, it became louder and louder, sweeping around the stadium: here was the soundtrack for a humiliation.

“Olé! Olé! Olé!” they roared and why not? Leeds were ripping Newcastle to pieces, knocking passes around them as if they were training-ground mannequins. Football has become a sport that leaves people increasingly vexed, but this was a night when – for the locals, at least – it was almost a throwback.

There was energy and ferocious tackling, a No 9 soaring like centre-forwards used to in the not-too-distant past and lots of goals as Leeds cut loose and abruptly ended whatever honeymoon Matthias Jaissle had been experiencing in charge of Newcastle.

“I suppose in football you can always find something to moan about,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, said. “But this was a top-class performance.”

It has felt suspiciously like Newcastle’s start has been like an overstuffed plastic shopping bag, the handles straining to the point of snapping. Eventually they fell asunder. Leeds ran all over them and were too smart, slick and hungry, not to mention ruthless. No wonder Jaissle had nowhere to go.

The home fans were adamant this was one of the best nights Leeds have experienced under Farke and if they were prepared to say as much, you had an obligation to listen. Forget how wretched Newcastle were, Leeds had produced a performance to enable imaginations to run wild.

Centre to it all was Ao Tanaka, with his desire to keep Leeds playing forward, but it felt wrong to talk about one man when you had the unstoppable Dominic Calvert-Lewin, who would be substituted to a standing ovation, and the ubiquitous James Justin, among others.

"He just cannot stop scoring at Elland Road" 🔥Dominic Calvert-Lewin makes it 2-0 to Leeds! pic.twitter.com/Pv1TEpc5Qj

The foundations are being put in around the stadium for a cavernous new West Stand, and Farke’s remit is to ensure that Leeds will be firmly established in the Premier League by the time it is completed in the summer of 2028.

To be fair to Farke, he has laid a sturdy base for this team to thrive and it felt before kick-off that this was going to be a big evening for Leeds, who had made a quietly encouraging start to the campaign and had negotiated three challenging away trips without defeat.

Big? It turned out to be spectacular. The first half was so one-sided that a boxing referee would not have allowed Newcastle to come out for the second, such was the pummelling they received; wave after wave of white-shirted raids left the visitors black and blue.

Aside from one little rick inside the opening 10 minutes, when James Trafford dithered and presented Yoane Wissa with a chance to mug him, Leeds were every bit as sensational as Newcastle were shocking, seizing on the opportunity to go on a rampage.

Leeds would have been in front after 11 minutes but Ethan Ampadu’s fierce drive battered into Calvert-Lewin’s legs and bounced away. Normally in such circumstances, players will wave an arm to berate their bad luck, but Ampadu, celebrating his 26th birthday, smiled: he, like everyone else, sensed what was coming.

Jayden Bogle, Justin and Nico Elvedi all had opportunities to open the scoring earlier, but eventually, they found the weak spot. Newcastle, who had lost the influential Nico González to a potential concussion, had replaced him with Sean Steur and what an influence he would have on matters.

On the half hour, Steur was a fraction too late getting out to close down Tanaka, whose shot ricocheted off him and to Lewis Miley, before looping away from Lukas Hornicek and dropping into the corner of the net in dam-busting fashion.

Ao Tanaka's deflected effort puts Leeds ahead! ⚪ pic.twitter.com/cYXVi3LOAO

Leeds were running even quicker by this point, pressing as if their lives depended on it and making tackles that were lustily acclaimed in the stands. Steur completely short-circuited in the bedlam and a ridiculous pass on the edge of his area was pounced upon by Bogle.

Out went a ball to Justin, whose cross was whipped into the penalty area, where Calvert-Lewin had climbed to get his head to it, though replays indicated his effort glanced off Bogle’s head – determining the true scorer will make for an interesting conversation.

Calvert-Lewin, at least, got the reward his efforts deserved on the cusp of half-time, spinning away from Miley and chopping inside Sven Botman before delivering the kind of finish that should make Thomas Tuchel take note when selecting his next England squad this week.

"They are relentless!"Dominic Calvert-Lewin caps off a dominant first-half from Leeds 💪 pic.twitter.com/S6kQykOMW9

The gloss, after those “olés”, was applied in the 59th minute when Noah Okafor put a realistic hue on the score, ramming in a finish in front of the Kop and leaving Newcastle open to the crudest mocking for the amount of money they have spent to resemble such a disorganised rabble.

A wonderful strike with equally brilliant celebrations from Noah Okafor! 🕺 pic.twitter.com/Ce1ueKtH4x

Bazoumana Touré, at least, scored a consolation goal, but Jaissle barely flickered as it went in and the emotion belonged to Farke, who thundered on to the pitch at the final whistle and sought out his captain, Ampadu, who had erred in allowing Newcastle’s substitute to profit.

“That was an unnecessary goal to concede and I so wanted us to keep a clean sheet,” Farke sighed. “We deserved a clean sheet and I couldn’t help myself. I had to tell him because I am sometimes a perfectionist. We must try to stay humble, but we can be an outstanding team.”

And this, for certain, was an outstanding night.

[It was brutal out there?] That’s football. That’s the Premier League. It was clear from the start and I have said it many times. We will have ups and downs and challenges all the way. Tonight we faced that challenge. It’s tough and difficult to digest. But there is a chance to learn out of that and there’s a long time until our next match at home and that is good.

It’s clear with our young squad that there will be ups and downs and you have to bring the fundamentals on the pitch against such a physical team. Leeds are so intense, we couldn’t match that physicality. There are other aspects of course but I don’t want to make excuses. We want to learn out of it and be better.

[Were you overwhelmed as a team?] No. If you don’t bring that physicality on the pitch, you struggle.

Exactly this [message to the players]. Bring your fundamentals and we build on it. [Can you bounce back from this in your next game?] Of course. [Is your confidence hit?] No

For each manager it would be a nightmare after such a game to concede so late and not have the well-deserved clean sheet. Of course I was not happy about the situation. Doesn’t take anything away from my boys who were magnificent. Terrific start with eight points but there’s never a perfect performance. There’s always something to moan about. At very rare points [in the season] I have to criticise [for conceding].

Energy, quality, good structure, in an out of possession, which is complicated against Newcastle, In pressing them you always have to be aware of their unbelievable pace and strength in counter-attacks. We found this balance today and in the first half particularly we were dominant.

We have a good fitness level now. Need to find the right triggers to press. It’s a lot of well-structured work on the training ground. We had more chances to score tonight but overall I am very happy with our performance.

[Calvert-Lewin being praised] It is well deserved. He is in outstanding shape and plays with lots of confidence. I expect him to lead the group with some other players. His work-rate is never in doubt and to me he is one of the best strikers in the league.

The ref told me at half-time that they’ve taken it off me. I didn’t know he [Bogle] was there to be fair. I just got up and went ‘Bang!’ It is what it is. I’ll take the assist!

I didn’t know anything about it [being given credit for the second goal]. I said to the ref, I don’t fancy telling him [Calvert-Lewin]. To be fair he’s still raging. He’s raging with the goal but happy with the result.

It’s about having an understanding with the players around you. With Dom up there, you know he’s going to win everything so you have to get the runners around him.

It’s about the rotation like today. When James Justin goes wider there’s space inside. Dom occupies two centre-backs so there’s always pockets.

Regardless of the scoreline it was a tough game physically. They’re a very good side. We take it game by game, not to get carried away. Everyone’s ambitious in their own way but we have to take it game by game.

A proper stuffing for Newcastle as Leeds continue to impress and climb up to third.

James pounces on a loose ball, dribbles infield from the right. No one bothers to close him down so he eventually has a shot, blazing over with his left from 20 yards.

Late free-kick for Leeds after Livramento bundled Aaronson over. Wilson chips from the left to the far post and Muharemovic heads it back acros goal looking for a team-mate but none had made the run.

Leeds 4 Newcastle 1 (Touré) No clean sheet for Leeds. Farke is fuming after the substitute exploits an error and scores with a left-foot shot that deflects off Justin.

Livramento drives the ball 60 yards looking for Barnes but the ball skids off the turf and into Trafford’s arms.

Crunching Bard tackle on Bamba sends the ball to James who lets fly from 22 yards into the shins of a Newcastle defender.

Bard is penalised for a trip on Barnes as the game peters out.

Ampadu and Bamba collide when fighting for a loose ball but there was nothing malicious in it.

Wissa escapes a booking for a snide kick at Muharemovic’s shin.

A debatable offside call which should have been left for VAR lets Trafford off the hook when he comes out of his area to clear a ball clipped over the top. He slices it to Toure and the ref stops the game but I think Bard was playing Wissa, who found Toure, onside.

Newcastle corner on the left headed out by Elvedi and Barnes recovers the ball to start another attack with the 18-yard line stacked with players. When the diagonal comes back from left to right Barnes heads it behind for a goalkick.

Willock hooks a half-volley on to the roof of the net.

Bard → GudmundssonAaronson → OkaforWilson → Tanaka

Newcastle free-kick for a trip on Willock. Hall takes and Leeds head it out for a throw-in.

Livramento improves the quality of crosses with two that at least find the middle of the box even if they were headed away by Elvedi and Justin respectively.

Newcastle are enjoying more possession but the crossing has been awful when they do get down the flanks, Touré the latest offender.

Barnes shoots down Trafford’s throat. Barnes had thrown himself down in the box moments earlier and there was a VAR check but there was nothing like the contact required to send him swan-diving on to the grass.

Wissa gets down the right and whips over a low cross but Willock’s touch was too heavy.

There was a piece in the Athletic today saying Newcastle pivoted to Hornicek instead of pursuing Trafford again because he had a very high ceiling and was younger. He hasn’t caught much here, dropping the ball even when he chooses not to punch.

Matthias Jaissle promised high intensity, high octane, front foot football when he was interviewed for the Newcastle job. He and sporting director Ross Wilson have repeated that promise several times since he was appointed. There has been no sign of it since the opening weekend against Liverpool.

Newcastle are passive, they look disorganised in midfield and weak at the back. Oh and they barely apply pressure let alone attack dangerously.

These are early days but this performance and result had been coming. A pretty brutal reality check after all the positive noise and bold predictions in pre-season. This defeat will drop Newcastle to 12th in the table, where they finished last season under Eddie Howe.

Leeds 4 Newcastle 0 (Okafor) Ampadu hurls it into the box. A defender heads it to the edge of the area where Okafor thumps a left-footed half-volley in off the right post.

A wonderful strike with equally brilliant celebrations from Noah Okafor! 🕺 pic.twitter.com/Ce1ueKtH4x

Livramento slides in to stop Okafor’s drive down the left, giving Leeds another opportunity to throw it long.

Triple change: Livramento → DedicTouré → Fernandez-PardoWillock → Murphy

Leeds catch Newcastle playing short from the back. Stach blindsides Steur 20 yards out, tackles him, cuts inside then bends a left foot shot into the side-netting.

After Hall stings Trafford’s palms with a strike from distance. Newcastle want a penalty when the ball hits Tanaka’s arm … but it was outside the area and then Murphy, in frustration, chops down Gudmundsson and takes the booking as an occupational hazard.

Elvedi sloppily gives the ball way to Wissa who tries to set Fernandez-Pardo through down the left. Justin sticks with him and Bogle mops up after Justin was tripped.

Gudmundsson does the upended beetle when he tries to break from the corner and collides with a Newcastle player. He claims he was fouled and wthrashes about like a RL player after he’s tackled. He continues to do a Rumpelstiltskin polka of peevishness towards the ref for a while.

Newcastle corner on the left that Trafford backpedals to tip behind for another.

No changes at half-time for Newcastle as they kick off. Leeds break through the middle quickly and Calvert-Lewin seems to push the ball past Botman and shapes to shoot before Steur slides in with a crucial tackle just inside the box.

The first goal is now an own goal. The explanation is that Tanaka’s shot was on target but the deflection from Steur meant it was going wide until it hit Miley.

Now the second goal has been credited to Bogle as Calvert-Lewin’s header struck the top of his head before it went in.

You could not say that this scoreline is undeserved. Newcastle are being demolished physically. The central midfield two – Steur and Miley – just don’t have the power to screen their defence.

Leeds 3 Newcastle 0 (Calvert-Lewin) Leeds are running all over Newcastle who seem physically flimsy. Calvert-Lewin chops in from the left on to a flick-on, the ball takes a deflection off the Newcastle captain and he steers it into the far corner with a right-foot shot.

"They are relentless!"Dominic Calvert-Lewin caps off a dominant first-half from Leeds 💪 pic.twitter.com/S6kQykOMW9

Calvert-Lewin is booked for catching Botman in the face with a straight arm rather than a swinging arm. ‘Reckless but not violent.’ Trafford had punchd the corner away at the back post to set Leeds off on a counter.

Tanaka gives the ball away carelessly in midfield and Newcastle work it to Wissa who chops inside past Elvedi, hangs out his own leg looking for contact and hits the deck. The ref waves play on and the ball runs to Barnes in the left of the area. He shapes to shoot but Muharemovic sprinted over to make a fine block-tackle, forcing it behind for a corner.

Newcastle are rocking here. They cannot win a tackle.

For those of us who have watched all Newcastle United’s games this season, this was coming. They do not have any consistent attacking threat, they do no create chances and they are not secure at the back either.

They’ve survived by converting the very few chances they create in games but they have not even had a shot in the first half here.

Leeds should be three up after Hornicek fumbled Gudmundsson’s shot from the left. The ball falls to Calvert-Lewin five yards out and he triesto dink it over the keeper who recovers well to smother it.

Leeds 2 Newcastle 0 (Calvert-Lewin) Newcastle try to play the ball out from the back, give it away cheaply to Bogle who feeds Justin haring down the right. He is ostensibly the right centre-back but he is a full-back by trade and stands up a perfect near-post cross that Calvert-Lewin hangs in the air to bury with the firmest of headers. In fact it transpires that his downward header struck Bogle and another deflection benefits rampant Leeds –162 seconds between the goals.

"He just cannot stop scoring at Elland Road" 🔥Dominic Calvert-Lewin makes it 2-0 to Leeds! pic.twitter.com/Pv1TEpc5Qj

Leeds 1 Newcastle 0 (Tanaka) Good move, spawny finish. Tanaka sprays a pass out to Okafor who drives at Dedic then picks out Tanaka who had held his run. He cushions the pass then lets fly. The ball hits Steur, deflects on to Miley and then loops into the right of the goal with Hornicek understandably stranded.

Ao Tanaka's deflected effort puts Leeds ahead! ⚪ pic.twitter.com/cYXVi3LOAO

Good tackle by Steur on Bogle stops the Leeds right-back flying forward after Calvert-Lewin’s flick-on.

Newcastle really are not afraid to launch the ball forward are they? Football tactics are constantly evolving and fashions come back around. What better way to play through a press than to bypass the midfield completely? The hope is it will also cause the centre-backs problems, get them facing their own goal under pressure from one of Newcastle’s rapid forward players in a foot race.

It almost worked a couple of times in the first half but it should be pointed out that the best direct/long ball teams of the past tended to have a striker who was dominant in the air. Newcastle do not currently have one which does limit their threat from flick ons.

Newcastle break from defending a long throw. Wissa carries it 60 yards but with Murphy and Fernadez-Pardo better placed, he tries to shoot from 25 yards and plinks it straight at Trafford, provoking an inevitable ‘Woooooooo’.

From the resulting long throw Elvedi is found at the back post, unmarked and attempts to volley it towards goal, missing the ball entirely. It was so wild that even the Leeds staff laugh at how inept it was.

Leeds have a corner when they use one of their signature moves, Bogle cutting in from the right across the back four to take a ball over the top. He controls it but cannot force it past Thiaw.

Hornicek claws out the corner to Bogle 18 yards out. He puts his laces through a volley that Hornicek parries up high and punches away when he has a second go.

Newcastle chip it long again, this time down the right. Gudmundsson holds off Murphy and Leeds will have the relief of a goal-kick.

Leeds are finding it hard now to play through Newcastle’s high press and the intensity with which they are hounding keeper and defenders.

Newcastle keep looking to use their pace with balls over the top for Wissa, Murphy and Fernandez-Pardo. Wissa closes Trafford down quickly again. He needs to release it with more urgency.

Gonzalez hs not recovered from being struck on the head by the ball and is being replaced by Steur as a concussion sub.

Justin heads over his own bar when Newcastle chip a long pass down the inside right. Wissa beats Muharemovic and tries to find Fernandez-Pardo but Justin got there first. Newcastle go short from the corner and Leeds force them back into their own half.

Terrific save from Hornicek down low to his right. Tanaka’s cross from the left found Justin creeping round the back on the right and heading across goal from the back post. Bogle swivelled and tried a sidewinder flick that was arrowing towards the bottom left corner until the keeper swooped to turn it away with his right hand.

Wissa is ticking, feeling he is getting nothing from the referee when challenging for the ball, the latest incident involving a collision with Justin which was 50-50.

Leeds have been the slicker of the two sides, their passing and movement causing the full-backs problems. Okafor dribbles down the left and centres. Stach lays it back to Ampadu who hammers a half-volley from 18 yards that poleaxes Calvert-Lewin who was in an offside position.

Newcastle fans sing ‘There’s only one Kevin Keegan’ as the visitors’ defence sweeps the ball around. When they knock the ball up the inisde-right channel Wissa is penalised for swinging his arm and catching Muharemovic in the mooey.

Wissa presses Trafford high and the goalkeeper is a bit too casual but gets away with it. His clearance bounces off the attacker’s shin and loops out to the right. Leeds shift it quickly out to the left with Gudmundsson and Okafor bombing forward. A vicious cross from the left-back hits a Newcastle leg, loops up and smaxks Gonzales flush in the face, knocking him off his feet. The ref stops play.

Two bad moments for Newcastle early on. Lewis Hall caught out by a simple run and pass behind him and then, from the resulting corner Mathias Fernandez-Pardo looked very fortunate, in my opinion, to avoid conceding a penalty for handball.

He got the benefit of the doubt presumably because the ball bounced up onto his hand as he tried to bring it under control and he did not intend to control it with his hand or knock it away. The handball law confuses me but there is a higher threshold now.

Stach tackles Wissa in the centre-circle. Wissa is playing behind Fernandez-Pardo. Ampadu receives a long pass over the top, coming back from an offside position in the nick of time.

Fernandez-Pardo’s outstretched left arm is struck in the penalty area with the ball after they win the header but the ref waves play on and stops the game for a foul on the new striker.

It’s never a problem to come to Elland Road and the singing of Marching On Together before kick-off makes this one of the top three atmospheres in the country, easily. There are problems with VAR, though, and the whole stadium has just seen the ball strike Matias Fernanzes-Pardo’s hand in the area. The reason it is a problem is because we have become conditioned to thinking every time a ball touches someone on the arm in the area, a penalty should be awarded. It is preposterous that faceless beaks have distorted the game so much.

Leeds kick off, attacking the South Stand, from left to right, as they always prefer to do. Justin and Bogle combine on the right and Bogle bends a pass inside HAll to Stach who chooses to cross rather than shoot. It hits Botman and goes out for a corner.

Leeds are in their home kit of white with yellow and blue pinstripe hoops, Newcastle in their navy away kit.

Anthony [Elanga] is injured. Unfortunately we have to investigate further how long he will be out but obviously we miss him. We wish him to come back as quickly as possible. It could be [a long-term injury] but he will get another MRI next week and then we’ll see.

Lewis Hall is the perfect player profile for how we play. he is a young lad still and we are very excited [that he has signed a new contract].

The start was not easy. We didn’t have lots of time to prepare for pre-season and that’s one reason we are happy and satisfied with the start. But there is potential and we will work hard on the margins we want to improve.

There will be a lot of excitement surrounding Mathias Fernandez-Pardo’s first start for Newcastle United following his deadline day move from Lille but also keep an eye on Jacob Murphy on the right wing.

Fernandez-Pardo starts with a clean slate at Newcastle, Murphy has a lot of baggage and he has been a popular online target for criticism over the last year or so.

Indeed, some sections of the fanbase were stunned Newcastle rejected a £15m offer from Nottingham Forest on deadline day for a player who has entered the final 12 months of his contract.

Murphy has his limitations, sure and he can be infuriating sometimes when he gives the ball away cheaply, but there is a reason Matthias Jaissle was adamant he could not be sold.

Part of that is due to the fact he does not have another specialist right winger behind Anthony Elanga who misses the Leeds game through injury.

But Murphy is also valued for his experience and his training ground presence. He has been at the club a long time, working under Rafa Benítez, Steve Bruce and Eddie Howe and is a boyhood Newcastle fan.

Jaissle was not willing to lose that from his dressing room. Ultimately, though, Murphy has to perform on the pitch to justify the faith shown in him.

There are not many other options to fill that position while Elanga is missing. Harvey Barnes does not like playing on the right, Amar Dedic is a full back and so is Tino Livramento.

This is an opportunity for Murphy to silence his detractors and prove the faith Jaissle has put in him is not misplaced. At the age of 31, he knows he is not the most popular or appreciated player at the club but he has never shirked or complained about that.

He formed a potent partnership with Alexander Isak when he was leading the line for Newcastle. Can he do the same with the new boy Fernandez-Pardo?

Mind you I remember his visit to Elland Road in 1982-83. Not for the faint hearted. In fact it was a disgrace when he was hit by a coin. And yet he was always gracious about Leeds and particularly fond of Don Revie. He was one of very few football people without a strong Leeds United connection who went to his funeral in 1989.

Apparently he was injured in training, the nature of the injury is unspecified.

Newcastle have made a very good start particularly in their transitional moments on the counter-attack. We have to be switched on today to get the next points.

After many years of suffering our supporters deserve it [high expectations]. It’s good but we are far away from not being humble. Our feet are on the ground. We know the second year is always difficult. We have made a good start and it is always important to ride the momentum as long as possible.

Eddie Howe has left a legacy and the culture he created is still around. Matthias has to work with it. They are unbeaten. they are very dangerous with many pacy players up front. It’s important not to lose the ball too easily and always be switched on against Newcastle.

Leeds United Trafford; Justin, Elvedi, Muharemovic; Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson; Stach, Okafor; Calvert-Lewin. Substitutes Zetterer, Bard, Bijol, Longstaff, Aaronson, Wilson, James, Bahoya, Nmecha.

Newcastle United (4-2-3-1) Hornicek; Dedic, Thiaw, Botman, Hall; González, L Miley; Murphy, Fernandez-Pardo, Barnes; Wissa. Substitutes Pope, Livramento, Schär, Bamba, Steur, Touré, Willock, Ramsey, M Miley.

Fernández-Pardo replaces Joe Willock and Murohy comes in for Elanga from the starters of the 2-2 draw with Bournemouth:

MFP starts at Elland Road! 🇧🇪 pic.twitter.com/b3Gsazcuaf

Farke names same side as the starting XI for the 1-1 draw with Brighton:

📋 Your #LUFC XI... pic.twitter.com/FG3gW13U8S

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of Leeds United vs Newcastle United, the last Premier League match of the fourth round of fixtures for the 2026-27 season. Both clubs have made unbeaten starts with one win and two draws each and a win today for wither would send them up to fourth. The two sides met at Elland Road in the third match of last season which ended in a 0-0 draw but the return fixture at St James’ Park was one of the games of the season, a ding-dong match that Leeds led 0-1, 1-2 and 2-3, the latter until the 91st minute and yet still lost 4-3.

The architect of that victory for Newcastle was the Leeds’ fans’ incubus, a player commonly known around Elland Road as ‘Harvey F------- Barnes’. His two goals that night were his sixth and seventh against Leeds in eight matches for Leicester and the Toon. Back in the last century and at the turn of this one, Alan Shearer scored 21 league goals in 23 games against Leeds for Blackburn Rovers and Newcastle, it can feel like one bogeyman passing the baton to another.

Newcastle’s sound form with their new model team this season has been based on searing pace and their ability on the counter whether with runners, in the case of Anthony Elanga, or with long diagonals against Tottenham that ripped a hole in the left side of their defence. Leeds rallied from being overrun by Brentford at half-time in their last home game to switch from three at the back to four and wrest back the initiative and while they reverted for the Brighton draw, in both games it was the introduction of Ao Tanaka in midfield that gave them control.

It is genuinely hard to decide whether the 6-3 defeat by Chelsea in the Carabao Cup from being 2-0 up at Stamford Bridge is significant to Leeds league form. One simplistic way of looking at it would be to say Leeds reserves were better than Chelsea’s reserves in the first half and Chelsea’s first-team were better than Leeds reserves and their shaky, debutant keeper in the second. But any similar defensive frailties tonight and there will be jitters over the next week before the international break. Newcastle, by contrast, toiled in their 1-0 victory over Millwall but the result glosses over a lack of incision for long spells of it.

Joe Rodon is out for Leeds for at least another month while Newcastle have changed to withholding information about their treatment room under Matthias Jaissle who says that it should be ‘confidential’. We do know that Joelinton, William Osula and Dan Burn are likely to still be out given the nature of their injuries but Amar Dedic, who came off at half-time at the New Den with a thigh or hamstring problem, may be back.

#1894. Rangers hitman makes impact off the bench but late goal sees team sink to record breaking low

Rangers striker Ryan Naderi continued his strong recent form but was denied a morale-boosting draw as a dramatic late goal saw Czechia slump to a record-breaking 2-1 defeat against Croatia in Osijek.

Already relegated to League B before the game, the visitors entered the clash without a win in eight, and had lost all five of their Nations League games, conceding 12 goals and scoring just twice.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Naderi, who opted to represent Czechia last month despite also being eligible to represent Germany and Bulgaria, made his international debut as a second-half substitute in a 3-1 defeat to world champions Spain in October before making his full debut against England at Wembley a few days later.

He had to be content with a place on the bench, though, as Czechia went in search of their first Nations League points against Croatia on Sunday. However, they started the game in the worst possible fashion, with veteran winger Ivan Perisic putting the home side ahead after just 87 seconds via a clinical left-footed strike from the edge of the penalty area.

Searching for a quickfire second, Croatia piled on the pressure following their early opener, but Czechia stood firm until half-time. Looking to restore parity, Czechia began to get back into the game after the restart, with Antonin Kinsky, Idris Hopi and Adam Hlozek all attempting to get past Barcelona stopper Dominik Livakovic in the home side’s net. With the game entering the final stages, Rangers forward Naderi was introduced in the 74th minute as a substitute for Christophe Kabongo, and he helped Czechia level the score shortly afterwards.

Scoring nine goals and assisting five more for Rangers this season, he was on the field just 10 minutes before he found strike partner Adam Hlozek in a dangerous scoring position. His initial effort was blocked, but Hlozek reacted quickest to rifle home a left-footed finish to level the level. However, just as it appeared that Naderi’s had helped his side steal a late point, Croatia restored their lead three minutes later through substitute Lovro Majer.

Taking a pass from Brighton centre-back Luka Vuskovic in the away side’s area, he drilled a low drive into the net to condemn Czechia to a seventh consecutive defeat and the worst losing streak in their history.

Beginning in the group stages of this summer’s World Cup in North America, Czechia’s slide began with a 3-0 defeat to Mexico and has carried straight through into a brutal Nations League campaign against Spain, England, and Croatia.

#1893. Wilson’s wondrous finish seals FA Trophy win as Eastbourne Borough close door on Curfews

Tyano Wilson, just 18, had been pitched into the action by manager Steve King on 74 minutes in a last attempt to break the deadlock ahead of a potential penalty shoot-out – and the young man seized his opportunity.

A pass into his feet, just inside the box. A touch, a swerve to the left, and just enough space and sight of goal. A fizzing left-foot shot that found the top corner with Chertsey keeper Luke Roberts clutching at thin air: 2-1 and the Sports had claimed a memorable victory.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

It had been a cracking contest, and the visitors had played a full part. Borough had slightly more of the ball and slightly the better chances, but after claiming a ludicrously early lead, they never put the game to bed – and a fateful red card, late in the first half, had put the home side at a disadvantage for an hour.

What a start for the Sports. After successfully defending two Chertsey corners in the first two minutes, the home side broke with Josh Rees through the right channel and Terrell Egbri blitzed down the touchline. He raced on to the pass, a touch, a delightful looped cross just too high for startled keeper Roberts, and there at the back post was Paul McCallum to head home.

But the Curfews – among the leaders in their own Southern Premier division – had not come south for a charabanc outing, and they responded strongly. Liam Nash saw his 25-yarder spilled for a Borough corner – from which Chertsey raced the length of the pitch and almost equalised.

The high pace was matched by some physical moments, too. Chertsey had copped one early yellow card, but they escaped sanctions for a couple of heavy challenges, a blatant handball and an obvious trip on Liam Nash in the area.

On the other hand, Freddie Carter was fortunate to escape without a card for one pretty blatant challenge on Nathan Minhas 20 minutes, and these marginal moments tend to even out. Chances were being traded like swap cards.

Then, a potentially game-changing moment. After an apparent elbow in Egbri’s face had been unpunished, Borough left-back Nathan Laleye did incur the ultimate sanction four minutes before half-time: a little wrestle with Chertsey danger man Minhas was judged a denial of a scoring opportunity – and Mr Black flourished red.

Arguably Carter – spared his own red card earlier – was in a covering position, but referees do not have multi-angle replays, and the Sports would have to play for almost an hour a man down. King responded at once by replacing Darren McQueen with full-back Elliott Johnson.

Alex Fisher, on a yellow card, escaped a second caution after first fouling Egbri and then kicking the ball away.

After half-time, Chertsey were on the front foot at once. Minhas put one effort too high and a second chance wide, but Borough were feeling anything but comfortable. The minutes were clicking away, painfully slowly for home supporters but a little anxiously for the Curfews – until exactly at the mid-point of the second half, the visitors had their chance.

Harry Phipps, working overtime at the heart of defence, tripped Leo Farruch, who had just spurned a priceless chance. A clear penalty, and Minhas seized the chance to equalise from the spot.

One-all, and as the Curfews pressed their one-man advantage, the Sports were digging deep. Their best chance seemed to be the penalty shoot-out – or could the ten men somehow snatch a winner?

Veteran semi-pros only grit their teeth and and resign themselves. But buoyant 18-year-olds, unleashed off the bench, seize the moment.

And Wilson, in those final 15 minutes, would claim the moment. Into added time, he took possession a yard inside the Chertsey area, shimmied left to open up a sight of goal, and smashed a dream of a shot into the top right corner. Despair for the Curfews, elation for the Sports.

#1891. When is the Nations League quarter-finals draw? TV and streaming details, plus how to watch

The group stage of the Nations League is almost at a close, with the final fixtures taking place this week across Europe.

Set to begin in March, sides from League A will have their sights set on lifting the Nations League title, while League B, C and D nations fight it out for promotion and relegation.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Won by Portugal last year, they claimed a second title with a penalty shootout win over Spain after playing out a thrilling 2-2 draw with Spain in Munich, Germany. Winners of the inaugural tournament in 2019, they are now the most successful team in Nations League history, ahead of Spain and France, who have one win each.

Want to know when the draw for the Nations League quarter-final takes place, who has qualified and when the games will take place? Here’s everything you need to know:

Get our daily football newsletter by clicking here.

The draw for the Nations League quarter-finals will take place on Friday, 20 November. The draw begins at 11am UK time and will take place at UEFA headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland.

As of November 15, the following teams have confirmed a place in the Nations League quarter-finals: France, Belgium, England, Portugal and Spain.

In total, eight teams qualify for the quarter-finals via League A. The four League A group winners are seeded and placed in Pot 1 of the draw, with the four League A group runners-up are placed in Pot 2 and unseeded. Each group winner is drawn against a runner-up from a different group. Teams from the same group cannot play each other in the quarter-finals.

Teams placed in Leagues B, C and D all compete for promotion and relegation, and are unable to qualify for the knockout stage of the competition.

The upcoming quarter-final ties will be played over two legs during the March 2027 international break. The seeded group winners will play the first leg away from home, with the second leg on home soil. First legs are scheduled to take place from 25–27 March 2027, and second legs follow from 28–30 March 2027.

The draw will not be broadcast in the UK and Ireland. However, they are several options to stream the draw live, which are detailed below.

If you want to stream the draw via your smart TV, laptop, tablet or mobile phone, the entire ceremony will be streamed for free via UEFA.tv and via the official UEFA YouTube channel.

#1890. Nones makes little piece of Oval history – and Eastbourne United make it three wins in a row

Common have had a poor start to the season, United quite the opposite, sitting in second place at the start of a day on which the latest addition to the ground was unveiled – an electronic scoreboard at the Seaside Road end.

Early on, there seemed to be a somewhat frantic attempt by most in the United team to be the one who registered the first goal on the new board, with Joe Overy looking like he had new batteries installed.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Four times he opened up the Common defence, but Callum Barlow, Ryan Blunt and Overy himself all shot agonisingly wide, and Jorge Nones had one well saved.

With 25 minutes gone, Barlow was hauled down in the box but the referee inexplicably waved play on. The ball was loose, everyone dived on it and Brett Patton’s sidefooted effort won a corner. Cometh the hour, cometh, well the boy - 35 minutes were showing on the new scoreboard as Nones kept a cool head to drive past Matt Crutwell to make it 1-0 to United. He will forever be the first scorer to have his name on the new board.

The second half proceeded with remarkably little incident – there was somehow an inevitability that if Common did too much, United would go and score, so a kind of detente broke out.

Deep into the second half, Alieu Secka had one of those moments that goalies specialise in, terrifying the crowd as a mix-up led to him scrambling to push the ball round for a corner.

The pressure was increasing and both teams probed more as United boss Anthony Storey rang the changes – Charlie Ball and James Stone had already joined the fray when James Hull replaced Nones. And 47 second later, Hull made it 2-0, breaking Common’s resistance completely and sending the Oval crowd home happy.

Nearly 250 braved the cold, and in a great atmosphere, football was the real winner as United prepared for Tuesday night’s visit to Bognor in the last 16 of the Sussex Senior Cup.

This Saturday Eastbourne United’s visitors are fourth-placed Guernsey, and it’s a 2pm kick-off at the Oval Arena.

#1889. Hearts boss Vrancken is playing with fire by turning the guns on his own players

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:17 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 12:26 EST, 10 November 2026

Not for the first time this season under Wouter Vrancken, Hearts suffered a complete and utter implosion as they were thrashed 5-2 at home to Falkirk last weekend.

This is a team who lost 6-0 to Sturm Graz over two legs in the Champions League qualifiers back at the start of the campaign.

A team who were then battered 6-1 away against Benfica in Lisbon in the Europa League qualifiers – and a team who were also thumped 7-1 against Celtic at Parkhead a few weeks ago.

Hearts also lost the derby to Hibs just over a week ago in the semi-finals of the Premier Sports Cup at Hampden.

Now comes an annihilation against Falkirk where Hearts were 4-0 down by half-time. What a shambolic way to lose a long unbeaten record at home.

Even accounting for what had gone before in some of those matches this season, what happened on Sunday at Tynecastle felt like a new low.

Hearts were a shambles. But what was even more alarming was the manager's inability to stop the bleeding and make any changes from the touchline.

All of which poses a very simple question. Have Hearts and Jamestown made a mistake with Vrancken? At the moment, he looks hopelessly one-dimensional.

But it was his post-match comments on Sunday afternoon which actually became even more alarming than the performance itself.

Wouter Vrancken was 'embarrassed' by Hearts' 5-2 home loss to Falkirk

Vrancken branded it 'embarrassing' and a 'disgrace'. He called his players 'childish' and basically insinuated that they lacked any spirit or character until the youngsters came off the bench.

In the midst of a horrendous injury crisis and with players dropping like flies, that is a very dangerous game for any manager to play. He threw them under a bus.

By publicly slaughtering his players like that during a time of adversity and when many of them are being asked to play out of position, he is playing with fire.

Those are the type of comments that could very easily lose a dressing room. His comments would have gone down like a lead balloon among the squad.

Hearts have had the best part of a dozen players missing through injury. Vrancken himself has branded it an injury crisis unlike any other he has experienced throughout his career.

But what is most curious in all of this is that Vrancken seems totally unwilling to engage in any self-reflection throughout all of this.

After the shellacking at Celtic Park a few weeks ago, he lamented the fact his team had made too many individual errors.

There was no acknowledgment that his system had set them up to fail. No acceptance that pressing Celtic man-for-man and leaving players one-v-one at the back was a huge part of the problem.

Since he arrived in the summer, Vrancken's preferred style of play has been front-foot attacking football. There have been times when it has clicked reasonably well.

When he had his key players fit, Hearts were a good watch. But when the guts of a full team were then ripped out due to injury, it has quickly disintegrated into chaos.

Continuing to demand the same high-pressing and attacking style of play without meaningful adjustment is not principled. It is naive, inflexible, and tactically illiterate.

When the structure collapses, as it did against Falkirk and in the 7-1 defeat at Celtic, the emphasis returns to individual mistakes rather than collective vulnerability created by the system itself.

It is a classic example of a manager publicly hanging his players out to dry rather than choosing to accept his own part in the wider failings.

Hearts are not in crisis yet. They still sit fourth in the table, just a point behind Falkirk. But this is a team who have clearly regressed from where they were last season.

Vrancken was hired on the basis that he could bring a more dynamic style of play and move the team forward from the platform left behind by Derek McInnes.

As written in these pages a few weeks ago after the defeat to Celtic, there is absolutely no prospect whatsoever of this Hearts team challenging for the title this time around.

The current combination of a horrendous injury list, a rigid tactical approach and increasingly pointed public criticism of the players is a dangerous mixture that threatens to undermine everything.

Scottish football's fixture congestion, the demands of European competition and the physical toll of the season have exposed the limits of Vrancken's one-dimensional plan.

Adaptation is not a betrayal of principles. It is a basic requirement of the job when circumstances change this dramatically.

The international break offers a brief window. A handful of bodies may return for Hearts' next fixture against Dundee at Dens Park.

The more important return would be a change in tone and a willingness to adapt the demands placed on those players left still standing.

Publicly branding his players as 'a disgrace' while refusing to acknowledge that the system itself is contributing to their vulnerability is a sure-fire way to get himself sacked.

Vrancken's Hearts squad has been ravaged by injuries this season

The manager is entitled to be angry. He is entitled to demand better. He is not entitled to ignore the context he is operating in or the effect his words will have on a group already stretched to breaking point.

Vrancken arrived with a clear identity and early promise. The test now is whether he can evolve that identity under pressure or whether he remains locked into one way of playing regardless of the resources available.

Hearts cannot afford the latter. Much more of this public slaughtering and the players will switch off. Vrancken will have lost them completely.

Players will run for a manager who shows understanding of their situation even while criticising their standards.

They will begin to switch off for one who appears to place the preservation of his methods above the protection of the group.

That is the risk Vrancken is running. It is a risk no manager in the middle of a crippling injury crisis can afford to take.
